Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 13, verses 1–2:

(p-168) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah al-Ra'd (Thunder)

This surah is Meccan, said Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Qatada said: it is Medinan, except for two verses: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck with calamity for what they have done, or it will settle near their home﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], and His saying, ﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains would be moved﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], to the end of the verse. This is related by al-Zahrawi. al-Mahdawi related from Qatada that the surah is Meccan except His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck with calamity for what they have done, or it will settle near their home﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], and His saying: ﴿And whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43]. In my view, the apparent position is that there is much that is Medinan in it, and everything that was revealed concerning 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl and Arbad ibn Rabi'a is Medinan. It has also been said that the surah is Medinan; this is related by Mundhir ibn Sa'id al-Ballluti, and Makki ibn Abi Talib mentioned it.

His saying, exalted and majestic is He:

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the verses of the Book; and that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, but most of the people do not believe. Allah is He who raised the heavens without pillars that you see; then He istawa' (established Himself) over the Throne and subjected the sun and the moon, each running for a specified term. He arranges the affair and details the signs, that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord﴾

The discussion concerning the openings of the surahs and the interpretations of that has already preceded. What is specific to this place from that is what Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "These letters are from His saying: Ana Allahu A'lamu wa Ara (I am Allah, the Knower and the Seer)." And whoever says: "The letters at the beginnings of the surahs are an example of the letters of the alphabet" says: the indication here by "Tilka" (those) is to the letters of the alphabet. On this view it is permissible that "al-Kitab" (the Book) refers to the Qur'an, and it is permissible that it refers to the Torah and the Gospel. "Alif Lam Mim Ra" on this view is an inception (mubtada'), (p-169) and "Tilka" is a second inception, and "Ayat" (verses) is the predicate of the second, and the sentence is the predicate of the first. On the view of Ibn 'Abbas concerning "Alif Lam Mim Ra", "Tilka" is an inception, and "Ayat" is a substitute (badal) for it, and the two interpretations of "al-Kitab" that preceded are admissible.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that which has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth.﴾ "Alladhi" (that which) is in the nominative case by inception, and "al-Haqq" (the truth) is its predicate. On this, according to the interpretation of those who take ﴿Alif Lam Mim Ra﴾ to be the letters of the alphabet, "Tilka" and "Ayat" are an inception and predicate. On the view of Ibn 'Abbas, "Alladhi" is a conjunction upon "Tilka", and "al-Haqq" is the predicate of "Tilka". If "al-Kitab" is intended to be the Qur'an, then what is meant by "alladhi unzila" (that which was revealed) is the entire Shari'a, both what the Qur'an includes of it and what it does not include. It is also admissible that "Alladhi" be in the genitive position as a conjunction upon "al-Kitab"; if, with that, you intend by "al-Kitab" the Qur'an, then the waw is the conjunction of an attribute to a single thing, as you say: "The dignified man and the wise man came to me," while you mean one person. From this is the saying of the poet:

To the king, the lordly one, and the son of the hero, and the lion of the battalion in the crush.

And if, with that, you intend by "al-Kitab" the Torah and the Gospel, then that is clear. If, with that, you interpret "Alif Lam Mim Ra" as the letters of the alphabet, you raise His saying "al-Haqq" by supposing an omitted inceptive (mubtada') whose estimate is: "He is the truth." If you interpret them as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said, then "al-Haqq" is the predicate of "Tilka". Whoever raises "al-Haqq" by supposing an inception stops at His saying: ﴿from your Lord﴾, and the rest of the verse is apparent and clear, if Allah wills.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is He who raised the heavens﴾, to the end of the verse. Since His saying: ﴿but most of the people do not believe﴾ included a rebuke of the disbelievers, He followed that with mention of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, whom one should be certain of, and with mention of the proofs that call to belief in Him. As for the pronoun in His saying "tarawnaha" (you see it), a group said it refers to "al-samawat" (the heavens), so "tarawnaha" on this view is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The majority of people said: the heavens have no pillars. Another group said the pronoun refers to "al-'amad" (pillars), so "tarawnaha" (p-170) on this view is an attribute of the pillars, and this group said: the heavens have pillars that are not visible. This is related by Mujahid and Qatada. Ibn 'Abbas said: "What makes you know that they are pillars that are not seen?" Some related that the pillars are the mountain of Qaf that encircles the earth, and the sky is upon it like a dome.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak, and the truth is that there are no pillars at all, since a pillar needs a pillar, and the matter would regress endlessly, so it must end at the Power. This is the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He holds back the sky from falling upon the earth except by His permission﴾ [al-Hajj: 65], and similar verses. Iyas ibn Mu'awiya said: the sky is vaulted over the earth like a dome. In the Mushaf of Ubayy, it reads "tarawnahu" with the pronoun in the masculine.

"Al-'amad" is a collective noun (ism jam') of 'amud (pillar), and the regular pattern for its plural is "'umud" with the three letters vowelled with damma, like rasul and rusul, shihab and shuhub, and others. From this root is the saying of al-Nabigha:

And he informed the jinn that I had permitted them, and they built Tadmur with slabs and pillars.

al-Tabari said: "al-'amad" (with a fatha on the ayn) is the plural of 'amud, just as adim (hide) is pluralized as adam," and this is not as he said. In Sibawayh's book, adam is a collective noun, and likewise the grammarians stated concerning 'amad; but Abu 'Ubayda mentioned the matter without certainty, and al-Tabari followed him. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "bi-ghayri 'umud" with a damma on the ayn.

His saying: "thumma" (then) here is for the conjunction of sentences, not for sequence, because the istiwa' over the Throne was before the raising of the heavens. In the Sahih, it is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Allah was and nothing was before Him, and His Throne was upon the water, then He created the heavens and the earth."

(p-171) The discussion concerning people's speech about the istiwa' has already preceded, and its summary is that Abu al-Ma'ali preferred that He established Himself by His subjugation and dominance. The Qadi Ibn al-Tayyib and others said: "istawa" in this place means "istawla" (took possession), and taking possession may be without subjugation; this is the difference between the two views. Sufyan said: He did an act which He named istiwa'. al-Farra' said: the Messenger of Allah "istawa" in this place as the Arabs say: "Zayd did such and such, then istawa towards me speaking to me," meaning he turned and intended. It was related to me from Abu al-Fadl ibn al-Nahwi that he said: "al-'Arsh" (the Throne) in this place is a verbal noun from 'arasha, as if he meant all created things. Abu Mansur mentioned from al-Khalil that al-'arsh means dominion (mulk), and this supports the direction of Abu al-Fadl ibn al-Nahwi when he said: "al-'Arsh is a verbal noun." This contradicts what people have followed, that "al-'Arsh" is the greatest of the created things, the entity that was upon the water, and before which is the Kursi. Also, one should examine Abu al-Fadl's meaning of istiwa' as close to what is the view of all. In al-Bukhari, it is related from Mujahid that he said: "The meaning: He rose over the Throne," and likewise is the expression of al-Tabari, and sound reflection repels this expression.

His saying: "wa sakhkhara" (and He subjected) is an alert to power, and "al-shams wa al-qamar" (the sun and the moon), within mentioning them, includes mention of the stars; for this reason He said: ﴿each running﴾, that is, each of what has the meaning of the sun and the moon in subjection. "Kull" (each) is a word that requires an addition, either apparent or estimated.

The specified term (ajal musamma) is the ending of the world and the corruption of this structure. It has been said: by His saying "li-ajal musamma" He means the limits which these created things do not exceed, that is, they run upon known traces.

(p-172) His saying: "yudabbiru" means: He decrees and executes. He expressed it by "tadbir" (management) to bring it near to understanding, since tadbir is only looking at the backs of affairs and their outcomes, and that is a attribute of humans. "Al-amr" (the affair) is general over all affairs and what passes in every moment in the heavens and the earth. Mujahid said: "yudabbiru al-amr" means: He decrees it alone. The majority read "yufassilu" (He details). al-Hasan read it with the nun of majesty, and al-Khaffaf and 'Abd al-Wahhab related it from Abu 'Amr, and Hubayra from Hafs. al-Mahdawi said: they did not differ concerning "yudabbiru". Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: al-Hasan read with the nun in both. The reasoning indicates that His saying "yufassilu al-ayat" is not in the sense of His saying "yudabbiru" in enumerating the signs; rather, since the signs were numerous, and among them is "yudabbiru al-amr", He informed that He details them, perhaps the disbelievers may be certain of the resurrection. "Al-ayat" here refers to what was mentioned in the verse and after it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 13, verses 3–4:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿It is He who spread out the earth and placed in it firm mountains and rivers, and of all the fruits He made in it two pairs, two kinds. He covers the night with the day. Surely in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾ ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts, and gardens of grapevines, and crops, and palm trees, both single-stemmed and multi-stemmed, watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Surely in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾

When the signs of the heavens were finished, He mentioned the signs of the earth. His words "spread out the earth" (madda al-ard) imply that it is flat (basita), not spherical (kuriyya), and this is the apparent meaning of the Sharia. The rawasi (sing. rasiya) are the firm mountains, from "rasa yarsu", meaning it became firm. From this is the words of the poet:

"Around it are the she-camels that are not driven away, and the grey-headed one, whom the slave-girl planted with the stone pestle."

The zawj (pair) in this verse means the kind and the type, not the familiar pair of two mates of animals and others. From this is His words: ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya-Sin 36] and so on. (p. 173) Similar to this verse is "And the earth — We spread it out..." in (Qaf). This verse implies that every fruit exists in two kinds. If it happens that a fruit has more than two kinds, this does not contradict the meaning of the verse.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "yughshi" with a sukun on the ghayn and a light shin. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr) read it with a fatha on the ghayn and a shadda on the shin. Mentioning one reading suffices for the other. The rest of the verse is clear.

It seems that the azwaj (pairs), which are meant as kinds, types and species, were so named because in every fruit there are two, one male or female. al-Farra' indicated this when quoted by al-Mahdawi, and others reported from him what implies that the meaning is complete at His words "al-thamarat" (the fruits), and then it begins: that He placed in the earth, from every male and female, two pairs.

His words ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts﴾: qita' is the plural of qit'a, which means parts. In this example he restricted them to those that are adjacent and close to one another, because the difference between those that are close is more remarkable. Al-Jumhur read "wa-jannatun" with a raf' (nominative), in coordination with "qita'", while al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "wa-jannatin" with a nasb (accusative) by an implied verb. It was also said that it is coordinated with "rawasi". Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs from 'Asim read "wa-zar'un wa-nakhilun sinwanun wa-ghayru sinwanin" with raf' throughout, in coordination with "qita'". The rest read with khafd (genitive) throughout, in coordination with "a'nabin", and he made the garden to be of grapevines. Whoever reads "al-zar'" with raf' then the garden in its literal sense is the land in which there are grapevines, and in this there is a figurative usage. From this is the words of the poet:

"As if my two eyes, in the two lower corners of a slain (gazelle)... from the water-skins that water a garden of withered (palm trees)."

That is, the palm trees of a garden, since only palms are described as suhuq (withered). Whoever reads "al-zar'" with khafd, then the gardens are from the totality of that, not from the crops alone, because a cultivated field is not called a garden unless it is mixed with trees.

"Sinwan" is the plural of sinw, which is a branch that grows with another from one root, and sometimes there are more than two branches. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "Sinwan" means gathered together, and "ghayru sinwan" means scattered one by one. From this is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The paternal uncle is the sinw of the father." It was narrated that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) was quick to quarrel with al-'Abbas, so he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I wanted to say something to al-'Abbas, but I remembered your position with him, so I kept silent." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on you, O 'Umar. The paternal uncle is the sinw of the father." The plural of sinw is sinwan, and it is a broken plural. Abu 'Ali said: the kasra on the sad in the singular is not the one in the plural, and it runs in the manner of "fulk" (ship). You say "sinw" and "sinwan" in the plural with tanwin on the nun and i'rab (grammatical inflection). 'Asim, in the narration of al-Qawwas from Hafs, read "sunwan" with a damma on the sad. Abu 'Ali said: it is like "dhi'b" and "dhu'ban" (wolf and wolves). This is the reading of Ibn Musarrif and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, and it is the dialect of Tamim and Qays. Kasr of the sad is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. al-Hasan and Qatada read "sanwan" with fatha on the sad, and it is a collective noun (ism jam') not a plural. A parallel to this word is "qabw" and "qabwan". The "sinwan" was specified in this verse because it is comparable to the adjacency of the pieces of land, in which the strangeness of the difference of food appears. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza, (p. 175) al-Kisa'i, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and the people of Makka read "tusqa" with a ta', and Hamza and al-Kisa'i inclined the qaf. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "yusqa" with a ya', meaning: what was mentioned is watered. Al-Jumhur read "nufaddilu" with a nun, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-yufaddilu" with a ya'. Ibn Muhaysin read "yusqa" and "yufaddilu" with ya' in both. Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Abu Haywa read "wa-yufaddalu" with a ya' and fatha on the dad, "ba'duha" with raf'. Abu Hatim said: I found it so in the wording of Yahya ibn Ya'mur in his mushaf, and he was the first who put dots on the mushafs.

"Al-ukul" is the name of what is eaten, with a damma on the hamza, while "al-akl" is the verbal noun. A group read "fi al-ukul" with a damma on the hamza and the kaf, and this was already discussed in al-Baqara.

al-Tabari reported from more than one (scholar), including Ibn 'Abbas and others: ﴿neighbouring tracts﴾ meaning: one is salty and the other is sweet, and similar to this statement. Qatada said: the meaning is: adjacent villages. This is an aspect of lesson (i'tibar). It is as if He said: "And in the earth are different tracts, distinguished by Allah with different qualities. They are watered with one water, but differ in what they produce." What appears from describing them as adjacent is only that they share one soil and one kind. The lesson in this is clearer, because although they agree in soil and water, the power and will of Allah make some of their produce excel others. As the Prophet (ﷺ) said when he was asked about this verse: "(The daqal, the Persian [variety], the sweet and the sour)." According to the first meaning, al-Hasan said: this is a parable that Allah struck for the hearts of the children of Adam. The earth was in the hand of the Merciful one as one clay, then He spread it out and it became adjacent pieces. One water descends on them from the sky, and this one brings forth a flower and a fruit, while that one brings forth a salt flat (sabkha), brine and filth. Likewise, people were created from Adam, and a reminder descended upon them from the sky. Some hearts softened and humbled, some hardened, some were distracted, and some trembled. al-Hasan said: By Allah, no one sat with the Qur'an without rising from it with an increase or a decrease. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it adds nothing for the wrongdoers except loss﴾ [al-Isra' 17:82]. The preference in the produce includes the tastes, colours, textures and other things.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 13, verses 3–4:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿It is He who spread out the earth and placed in it firm mountains and rivers, and of all the fruits He made in it two pairs, two kinds. He covers the night with the day. Surely in that are signs for a people who reflect.﴾ ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts, and gardens of grapevines, and crops, and palm trees, both single-stemmed and multi-stemmed, watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in fruit. Surely in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾

When the signs of the heavens were finished, He mentioned the signs of the earth. His words "spread out the earth" (madda al-ard) imply that it is flat (basita), not spherical (kuriyya), and this is the apparent meaning of the Sharia. The rawasi (sing. rasiya) are the firm mountains, from "rasa yarsu", meaning it became firm. From this is the words of the poet:

"Around it are the she-camels that are not driven away, and the grey-headed one, whom the slave-girl planted with the stone pestle."

The zawj (pair) in this verse means the kind and the type, not the familiar pair of two mates of animals and others. From this is His words: ﴿Glory be to He who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya-Sin 36] and so on. (p. 173) Similar to this verse is "And the earth — We spread it out..." in (Qaf). This verse implies that every fruit exists in two kinds. If it happens that a fruit has more than two kinds, this does not contradict the meaning of the verse.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "yughshi" with a sukun on the ghayn and a light shin. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr) read it with a fatha on the ghayn and a shadda on the shin. Mentioning one reading suffices for the other. The rest of the verse is clear.

It seems that the azwaj (pairs), which are meant as kinds, types and species, were so named because in every fruit there are two, one male or female. al-Farra' indicated this when quoted by al-Mahdawi, and others reported from him what implies that the meaning is complete at His words "al-thamarat" (the fruits), and then it begins: that He placed in the earth, from every male and female, two pairs.

His words ﴿And in the earth are neighbouring tracts﴾: qita' is the plural of qit'a, which means parts. In this example he restricted them to those that are adjacent and close to one another, because the difference between those that are close is more remarkable. Al-Jumhur read "wa-jannatun" with a raf' (nominative), in coordination with "qita'", while al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "wa-jannatin" with a nasb (accusative) by an implied verb. It was also said that it is coordinated with "rawasi". Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs from 'Asim read "wa-zar'un wa-nakhilun sinwanun wa-ghayru sinwanin" with raf' throughout, in coordination with "qita'". The rest read with khafd (genitive) throughout, in coordination with "a'nabin", and he made the garden to be of grapevines. Whoever reads "al-zar'" with raf' then the garden in its literal sense is the land in which there are grapevines, and in this there is a figurative usage. From this is the words of the poet:

"As if my two eyes, in the two lower corners of a slain (gazelle)... from the water-skins that water a garden of withered (palm trees)."

That is, the palm trees of a garden, since only palms are described as suhuq (withered). Whoever reads "al-zar'" with khafd, then the gardens are from the totality of that, not from the crops alone, because a cultivated field is not called a garden unless it is mixed with trees.

"Sinwan" is the plural of sinw, which is a branch that grows with another from one root, and sometimes there are more than two branches. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "Sinwan" means gathered together, and "ghayru sinwan" means scattered one by one. From this is the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The paternal uncle is the sinw of the father." It was narrated that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) was quick to quarrel with al-'Abbas, so he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I wanted to say something to al-'Abbas, but I remembered your position with him, so I kept silent." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on you, O 'Umar. The paternal uncle is the sinw of the father." The plural of sinw is sinwan, and it is a broken plural. Abu 'Ali said: the kasra on the sad in the singular is not the one in the plural, and it runs in the manner of "fulk" (ship). You say "sinw" and "sinwan" in the plural with tanwin on the nun and i'rab (grammatical inflection). 'Asim, in the narration of al-Qawwas from Hafs, read "sunwan" with a damma on the sad. Abu 'Ali said: it is like "dhi'b" and "dhu'ban" (wolf and wolves). This is the reading of Ibn Musarrif and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, and it is the dialect of Tamim and Qays. Kasr of the sad is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. al-Hasan and Qatada read "sanwan" with fatha on the sad, and it is a collective noun (ism jam') not a plural. A parallel to this word is "qabw" and "qabwan". The "sinwan" was specified in this verse because it is comparable to the adjacency of the pieces of land, in which the strangeness of the difference of food appears. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza, (p. 175) al-Kisa'i, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far and the people of Makka read "tusqa" with a ta', and Hamza and al-Kisa'i inclined the qaf. 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "yusqa" with a ya', meaning: what was mentioned is watered. Al-Jumhur read "nufaddilu" with a nun, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-yufaddilu" with a ya'. Ibn Muhaysin read "yusqa" and "yufaddilu" with ya' in both. Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Abu Haywa read "wa-yufaddalu" with a ya' and fatha on the dad, "ba'duha" with raf'. Abu Hatim said: I found it so in the wording of Yahya ibn Ya'mur in his mushaf, and he was the first who put dots on the mushafs.

"Al-ukul" is the name of what is eaten, with a damma on the hamza, while "al-akl" is the verbal noun. A group read "fi al-ukul" with a damma on the hamza and the kaf, and this was already discussed in al-Baqara.

al-Tabari reported from more than one (scholar), including Ibn 'Abbas and others: ﴿neighbouring tracts﴾ meaning: one is salty and the other is sweet, and similar to this statement. Qatada said: the meaning is: adjacent villages. This is an aspect of lesson (i'tibar). It is as if He said: "And in the earth are different tracts, distinguished by Allah with different qualities. They are watered with one water, but differ in what they produce." What appears from describing them as adjacent is only that they share one soil and one kind. The lesson in this is clearer, because although they agree in soil and water, the power and will of Allah make some of their produce excel others. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 13, verses 5–7:**

[Verse] His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?" Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord. Those will have shackles around their necks, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good, although exemplary punishments have already passed before them. And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing, and indeed, your Lord is severe in punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide.﴾

This is a verse of rebuke for the disbelievers. That is, "And if you are amazed, O Muhammad, at their ignorance and their turning away from the truth, then they deserve that, and it is amazing and strange." What is meant is their saying: "Shall we return to a new creation after we have become dust?" The wording may also bear another sense: "And if you are increasing in amazement, then come, for among the most amazing things is their saying."

The readers differed over the recitation of His saying ﴿أإذا كُنّا تُرابًا﴾ (ʼa-ʼidhā kunnā turābā, "When we are dust?"). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "ʼa-ʼidhā kunnā turābā ʼa-ʼinnā la-fī khalqin jadīdin" all with interrogation, except that Abu 'Amr elongated the hamza and then came with a silent yā', while Ibn Kathir came with a silent yā' after the hamza without elongation. Nafi' recited "ʼayðā kunnā turābā" like Abu 'Amr, and the reports from him differed regarding the elongation. He recited "ʼinnā la-fī khalqin jadīdin" with a kasra, as a statement. Al-Kisa'i agreed with him in dispensing with the interrogative in the second part because of the first, except that he pronounced two hamzas. 'Asim and Hamza recited "ʼa-ʼidhā kunnā turābā ʼa-ʼinnā" with two hamzas in them. Ibn 'Amir recited "idhā kunnā turābā" with a kasra on the alif and without interrogation, "ʼā-ʼinnā," with a hamza, then elongation, then a hamza.

As for whoever recited with the two interrogatives, that is for emphasis, inquiry and insistence on this supposition. Whoever used the interrogative only in the first part, the intended interrogation is the second position, and "idhā" (when) is an adverbial complement to it. "Idhā" is in the accusative position governed by a suppressed verb whose estimated form is: "Will we be resurrected, or gathered, when?" Whoever used the interrogative only in the second part, it is clear. The reference of "ʼulāʼika" (those) is to the people who said: ﴿ʼa-ʼidhā kunnā turābā﴾, and that statement is only the affirmation of one determined in denial and rejection of the resurrection, so for this reason He judged them to be disbelievers.

His saying: ﴿وَأُولَئِكَ الأغْلالُ﴾ (wa-ʼulāʼika al-aghlālu, "and those, the shackles") may bear two meanings. The first is the literal one: that He informed of the presence of shackles around their necks in the Hereafter. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إذِ الأغْلالُ في أعْناقِهِمْ والسَلاسِلُ﴾ ("when the shackles are around their necks, and the chains," Ghafir: 71). The second is that it is metaphorical, and that He informed of their being shackled from faith. In that case, it operates in the manner of sealing and stamping upon the hearts, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنّا جَعَلْنا في أعْناقِهِمْ أغْلالا فَهي إلى الأذْقانِ، فَهم مُقْمَحُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks, and they reach to the chins, so they are held up," Ya-Sin: 8). The rest of the verse is clear. Some people said: "The shackles here are an expression for deeds, that is, their corrupt deeds are around their necks like shackles."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The clarification of this is in the second interpretation that we mentioned.

His exalted saying: ﴿وَيَسْتَعْجِلُونَكَ بِالسَيِّئَةِ قَبْلَ الحَسَنَةِ﴾ ("And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good"), to the end of the verse. This is a verse clarifying their error in wishing for calamities and seeking the falling of fragments from the sky or stones raining down upon them, and the like, although such things passed among the nations and descended upon many people. Had that never descended at all, they would have had an excuse.

"Al-mathulāt" (exemplary punishments) is the plural of "mathula," like "sumra" and "sumurāt," and "ṣadaqa" and "ṣadaqāt." The majority recited "al-mathulāt" with a fatha on the mīm and a ḍamma on the thāʼ. Mujahid recited with a fatha on the mīm and the thāʼ, and that is the plural of "mathala," meaning in the Hereafter, in the sense of a threat of punishment. ʻĪsā ibn ʻUmar recited "al-muthulāt" with a ḍamma on the mīm and the thāʼ, and it was reported from Abu 'Amr. Yahya ibn Wathhab recited "al-muthlāt" with a ḍamma on the mīm and a sukūn on the thāʼ, and these two are plurals of "muthla." Talha ibn Musarrif recited "al-mathlāt" with a fatha on the mīm and a sukūn on the thāʼ.

Then He gave hope by His saying: ﴿وَإنَّ رَبَّكَ لَذُو مَغْفِرَةٍ لِلنّاسِ عَلى ظُلْمِهِمْ﴾ ("And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing"). Al-Tabari said: its meaning is in the Hereafter. Some people said: the meaning is: when they repent, and "severe in punishment" is when they disbelieve.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of forgiveness here is only: His concealing it in this world and His granting respite to the disbelievers. Do you not see the facilitation in the wording "maghfira," and that it is indefinite and diminished, and there is no emphasis in it as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَإنِّي لَغَفّارٌ لِمَن تابَ وآمَنَ﴾ ("And indeed, I am Forgiving to whoever repents and believes," Ta-Ha: 82)? The pattern of the verse indicates this. Do you not see His judgment against them with the Fire? Then He said: "And they ask you to hasten," so when the evil of their deed became apparent, the punishment of them became necessary in the mind of the hearer, so He informed of His way with the nations, and that He grants respite despite the wrongdoing of disbelief. And nothing has come in the Sharia that Allah, exalted is He, forgives the wrongdoing of the servants.

Then He frightened by His saying: ﴿وَإنَّ رَبَّكَ لَشَدِيدُ العِقابِ﴾ ("And indeed, your Lord is severe in punishment"). Ibn al-Musayyab said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Were it not for Allah's pardon and His forgiveness, no one would have wished for life, and were it not for His punishment, everyone would have become complacent." Ibn ʻAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "There is nothing in the Qur'an more hopeful than this verse." And "al-mathulāt" are the deterrent punishments that make a person an example to be cited, and from it comes "tamthīl" (mutilation) of the slain, and from it the "muthla" (mutilation) of slaves.

His exalted saying: ﴿وَيَقُولُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا﴾ ("And those who disbelieve say"), to the end of the verse. This is a verse of disparagement of their extravagant demands, which Allah did not bring about as a custom except for the nation whose punishment and annihilation He had decreed. The "āya" (sign) here refers to the things that Quraysh named, such as an angel and a treasure and other than that. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed him that he is a warner, and this report is intended in its wording, and all people in its meaning.

The exegetes differed over His saying: ﴿وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هادٍ﴾ ("and for every people there is a guide"). ʻIkrima and Abu al-Duha said: the intended "guide" is Muhammad, peace be upon him. "Hād" is conjoined to "munḏir" (warner), as if He said: "You are only a warner and a guide for every people." This meaning then accords with the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "I have been sent to the red and the black." And "hād" according to this in this verse means one who calls to the path of guidance. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: "You are only a warner, and for every nation that passed there was a guide, that is, a prophet who called them. The purpose: so your affair, O Muhammad, is not novel or strange," and this resembles the aim of the verse. A group said: "The guide in this verse is Allah, mighty and majestic," which was reported from Ibn ʻAbbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Jubayr. And "hād" according to this means: one who originates guidance, and it is applied with this meaning, and it is known that Allah, exalted is He, is the Guide from other than this place. A group said: "The guide is ʻAlī ibn Abi Talib," and it was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), via Ibn ʻAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he recited this verse while ʻAlī was present, and he gestured with his hand to the shoulder of ʻAlī and said: ("You are the guide, O ʻAlī, through you the guided will be guided after me.")

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What resembles it, if this is authentic, is that the Prophet (ﷺ) only made ʻAlī an example of the scholars of the nation and its guides to the religion, as if he said: "O ʻAlī, you and your kind." Thus Abu Bakr, ʻUmar, ʻUthman, and the rest of the scholars of the Companions, may the pleasure of Allah be upon them all, enter into this, and likewise from every age. The meaning according to this is: "You, O Muhammad, are only a warner, and for every people, in the past and the present, there are shepherds and guides to good." The first opinion is the most probable interpretation of the verse.

[Verse] His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And if you are amazed, then amazing is their saying: "When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?" Those are the ones who disbelieved in their Lord. Those will have shackles around their necks, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ ﴿And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good, although exemplary punishments have already passed before them. And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind despite their wrongdoing, and indeed, your Lord is severe in punishment.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people there is a guide.﴾

This is a verse of rebuke for the disbelievers. That is, "And if you are amazed, O Muhammad, at their ignorance and their turning away from the truth, then they deserve that, and it is amazing and strange." What is meant is their saying: "Shall we return to a new creation after we have become dust?" The wording may also bear another sense: "And if you are increasing in amazement, then come, for among the most amazing things is their saying."

The readers differed over the recitation of His saying ﴿أإذا كُنّا تُرابًا﴾ (ʼa-ʼidhā kunnā turābā, "When we are dust?"). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "ʼa-ʼidhā kunnā turābā ʼa-ʼinnā la-fī khalqin jadīdin" all with interrogation, except that Abu 'Amr elongated the hamza and then came with a silent yā', while Ibn Kathir came with a silent yā' after the hamza without elongation. Nafi' recited "ʼayðā kunnā turābā" like Abu 'Amr, and the reports from him differed regarding the elongation. He recited "ʼinnā la-fī khalqin jadīdin" with a kasra, as a statement. Al-Kisa'i agreed with him in dispensing with the interrogative in the second part because of the first, except that he pronounced two hamzas. 'Asim and Hamza recited "ʼa-ʼidhā kunnā turābā ʼa-ʼinnā" with two hamzas in them. Ibn 'Amir recited "idhā kunnā turābā" with a kasra on the alif and without interrogation, "ʼā-ʼinnā," with a hamza, then elongation, then a hamza.

As for whoever recited with the two interrogatives, that is for emphasis, inquiry and insistence on this supposition. Whoever used the interrogative only in the first part, the intended interrogation is the second position, and "idhā" (when) is an adverbial complement to it. "Idhā" is in the accusative position governed by a suppressed verb whose estimated form is: "Will we be resurrected, or gathered, when?" Whoever used the interrogative only in the second part, it is clear. The reference of "ʼulāʼika" (those) is to the people who said: ﴿ʼa-ʼidhā kunnā turābā﴾, and that statement is only the affirmation of one determined in denial and rejection of the resurrection, so for this reason He judged them to be disbelievers.

The first is the literal one: that He informed of the presence of shackles around their necks in the Hereafter. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إذِ الأغْلالُ في أعْناقِهِمْ والسَلاسِلُ﴾ ("when the shackles are around their necks, and the chains," Ghafir: 71). The second is that it is metaphorical, and that He informed of their being shackled from faith. In that case, it operates in the manner of sealing and stamping upon the hearts, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنّا جَعَلْنا في أعْناقِهِمْ أغْلالا فَهي إلى الأذْقانِ، فَهم مُقْمَحُونَ﴾ ("Indeed, We have put shackles around their necks, and they reach to the chins, so they are held up," Ya-Sin: 8). The rest of the verse is clear. Some people said: "The shackles here are an expression for deeds, that is, their corrupt deeds are around their necks like shackles."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The clarification of this is in the second interpretation that we mentioned.

His exalted saying: ﴿وَيَسْتَعْجِلُونَكَ بِالسَيِّئَةِ قَبْلَ الحَسَنَةِ﴾ ("And they ask you to hasten the evil before the good"), to the end of the verse. This is a verse clarifying their error in wishing for calamities and seeking the falling of fragments from the sky or stones raining down upon them, and the like, although such things passed among the nations and descended upon many people. Had that never descended at all, they would have had an excuse.

Talha ibn Musarrif recited "al-mathlāt" with a fatha on the mīm and a sukūn on the thāʼ.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 13, verses 8–10:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying:

﴿Allah knows what every female bears, and what the wombs diminish and what they increase. And everything with Him is by measure.﴾ ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Exalted.﴾ ﴿It is equal to Him whether one of you conceals speech or speaks aloud, and whether one hides by night or goes forth freely by day.﴾

When the disbelievers' astonishment and their denial of resurrection from the graves had preceded, Allah in these verses set forth the examples that call attention to the power of Allah, blessed and exalted, and that make resurrection possible. Among these is this one, one of the five keys to the unseen (mafatih al-ghayb). It is that Allah, blessed and exalted, alone possesses knowledge of what every female of every kind of animal carries of embryos. This beginning shows that re-creation is not difficult for the One who is capable of the first creation.

The "mā" in His saying, ﴿mā taḥmilu﴾ ("what she carries"), may be a relative pronoun (bi-ma'na alladhi) functioning as the object of "ya'lamu" (knows). It may be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), also functioning as the object of "ya'lamu." It may also be an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence, with "taḥmilu" as the predicate, though this aspect is weak. In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b (a codex attributed to a companion), the reading is: "mā taḥmilu kullu unthā wa mā taḍa'u" ("what every female carries and what she delivers").

His saying, ﴿wa mā taghīḍu al-arḥām﴾ ("and what the wombs diminish"), means: what they decrease. This derives from the meaning of ﴿wa ghīḍa al-mā'u﴾ ("and the water subsided") [Hud: 44], which is from the sense of drying up (nuḍūb). Here it means the removal and departure of something from the womb. When His saying ﴿wa mā tazdādu﴾ ("and what they increase") corresponds to it, it is interpreted as the sense of decrease. Then the commentators differed about the form of the increase and decrease. Mujahid said: The diminishing of the womb is that she sheds blood upon the pregnancy. When that happens, the child becomes weak in the womb and pale. When the pregnant woman completes nine months and does not deliver, the child remains in her womb for an additional period in which he completes from his body and health what was lost through the shedding of blood. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿wa mā taghīḍu al-arḥām wa mā tazdād﴾.

Most commentators hold that the diminishing of the womb is the release of blood upon the pregnancy. Some people held that its diminishing is the drying up of blood in it and its retention after the customary release through menstruation (ḥayḍ). Then His saying ﴿wa mā tazdād﴾ after that would run in the sense of "taghīḍ" without correspondence. Rather, the diminishing of the womb means an increase in it. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The diminishing of the womb is that the woman miscarries the child, and the increase is that she delivers him after a full term, complete in his creation. Qatada said: The diminishing is miscarriage (siqt), and the increase is that the child remains beyond nine months.

His saying, ﴿wa kullu shay'﴾ ("and everything"), is a general term covering everything to which measure applies.

Al-ghayb ("the unseen") is what is hidden from perception, and al-shahāda ("the witnessed") is what is observed among matters. He placed the verbal nouns in the place of the things, each of which must have one of the two states.

His saying "al-Kabīr" ("the Great") is an attribute of absolute magnification. "Al-Mutaʿāl" ("the Exalted") derives from ʿulūw (elevation). The readers differed about pausing (waqf) on "al-Mutaʿāl." Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr (in some of what is reported from him) pronounced the final yā' in both continuation (waṣl) and pause (waqf). The rest did not pronounce it in either continuation or pause. Its pronunciation is the normal and standard practice. Sibawayh regarded its omission at verse-endings (fawāṣil), as in this verse, as easy, by analogy with rhymes (qawāfī) in poetry. Its omission outside verse-endings or poetry is considered ugly. The reason is that since tanwīn (nunation) always replaces the definite article "al-," and this yā' is omitted along with tanwīn, it was acceptable to omit it along with what replaces it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Connected with this verse is a point of jurisprudence (fiqh) worth mentioning.

Among these is the disagreement of the jurists about the blood a pregnant woman sees. Malik and his companions, al-Shafi'i and his companions, and a group held that it is menstruation (ḥayḍ). A great group said: It is not menstruation. If it were menstruation, clearing the womb of an enslaved woman by menstruation (istibrā') would not be valid, and this is a consensus (ijmā'). It is reported from Malik in the book of Muhammad (Ibn al-Mawwaz) what implies that it is not menstruation. Among this is that the community (umma) is in consensus that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months. This is derived from His saying: ﴿wa ḥamluhu wa fiṣāluhu thalāthūna shahran﴾ ("his gestation and weaning are thirty months") [al-Ahqaf: 15], together with His saying, ﴿wal-wālidātu yurḍi'na awlādahunna ḥawlayni kāmilayni﴾ ("and mothers breastfeed their children for two complete years") [al-Baqara: 233]. These six months are by the lunar crescents (al-ahilla), like the rest of the months of the Shari'a. For this reason it has been reported within the school (madhhab) from some companions of Malik, and I think it is in the book of Ibn Harith, that if three days are lacking from the six months, the child is still attributed to the father, due to the cause of the lunar months being deficient or complete.

As for the maximum period of pregnancy (akthar al-ḥaml), it has been disputed. It was said: nine months, but this is weak. ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and a group of scholars said: its maximum is two years. A group said: three years. In al-Mudawwana: four years and five years. Ibn Shihab and others said: seven years. It is reported that the wife of Ibn ʿAjlan gave birth after seven years. It is reported that al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim remained in the womb for two years. He said: "I was born and my front teeth had already come out." It is reported that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan was born after six months.

His saying, ﴿sawāʾun minkum﴾ ("it is equal from among you"), and the rest of the verse: "sawāʾ" is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It requires after it two things that are alike. Its being in the nominative is as the predicate of the subject "man" (whoever). A verbal noun cannot be a predicate except with an implied element, as al-Khansa said:

……………………

*"Indeed she is only advance and retreat"*

meaning: possessor of advance and retreat. One group said: here the meaning is "dhū sawāʾ" (one who is equal). Al-Zajjaj said: the use of "sawāʾ" in Arabic speech became frequent until it functioned like an active participle, so it needs no implied element.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view it is like ʿadl (justice) and zūr (falsehood) and ḍayf (guest), in that they are used as descriptive nouns.

(p. 183) Another group said: the meaning is "mustawin minkum" (equal among you), so it needs no implied element. Sibawayh regarded this as weak, because it begins with an indefinite noun (nakira). The meaning of this verse: it is balanced among you in Allah's encompassment and knowledge, whether one conceals his speech so that he whispers it to himself, or speaks it aloud so that he makes it heard. Nothing is hidden from Allah, the Exalted.

His saying, ﴿wa man huwa mustakhfin bil-layl﴾ ("and whoever hides by night"), means: whoever is in the utmost concealment at night, and whoever moves about freely by day going on his way, are equal in the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted, and in His encompassment of both. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid took a meaning that implies: the one who hides by night and goes forth by day is one man, suspicious by night, and displaying innocence by day in his dealings with people. So this is one category, one who made the night a time of rest. The meaning: this one and the one whose whole affair is one, innocent of suspicion, are equal in Allah's awareness of all of them. This interpretation is supported by the conjunction of "sārib" without repeating "man," and its omission is not found except in poetic necessity.

"Sārib" in the language means one who acts as he wishes. Of this is the poet's saying:

*"I see every people has tied the fetter of their stallion,*
*but we have loosed its fetter, so it roams free"*

meaning: unrestrained, not turned away from any direction. This is a man who boasts of the might of his people. Of this is also the saying of another:

*"However you go, you went, though you were not one who strays,*
*and dreams bring near what is not near"*

The verse may contain three categories: one who conceals speech is one extreme, one who speaks aloud is an extreme opposite to the first, and the third is a middle one, changeable, who disobeys by night secretly and displays innocence by day. The meaning of the verse extends to deeds as well. Qutrub, as transmitted by al-Zajjaj, said: "mustakhfin" means apparent, from their saying "khafaytu al-shay'" when one reveals a thing. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"It (the rain) uncovered them from their clouds, as if*
*the rain of an evening, pouring down, had revealed them"*

He said: "sārib" means one hidden in a cave (sirb).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Although this view has a clear connection to the language, it is weak, because the pairing of night with "mustakhfin" and day with "sārib" refutes this view.

Among these is the disagreement of the jurists about the blood a pregnant woman sees. Malik and his companions, al-Shafi'i and his companions, and a group held that it is menstruation (ḥayḍ). A great group said: It is not menstruation. If it were menstruation, clearing the womb of an enslaved woman by menstruation (istibrā') would not be valid, and this is a consensus (ijmā'). It is reported from Malik in the book of Muhammad (Ibn al-Mawwaz) what implies that it is not menstruation. Among this is that the community (umma) is in consensus that the minimum period of pregnancy is six months. This is derived from His saying: ﴿wa ḥamluhu wa fiṣāluhu thalāthūna shahran﴾ ("his gestation and weaning are thirty months") [al-Ahqaf: 15], together with His saying, ﴿wal-wālidātu yurḍi'na awlādahunna ḥawlayni kāmilayni﴾ ("and mothers breastfeed their children for two complete years") [al-Baqara: 233]. These six months are by the lunar crescents (al-ahilla), like the rest of the months of the Shari'a. For this reason it has been reported within the school (madhhab) from some companions of Malik, and I think it is in the book of Ibn Harith, that if three days are lacking from the six months, the child is still attributed to the father, due to the cause of the lunar months being deficient or complete.

As for the maximum period of pregnancy (akthar al-ḥaml), it has been disputed. It was said: nine months, but this is weak. ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and a group of scholars said: its maximum is two years. A group said: three years. In al-Mudawwana: four years and five years. Ibn Shihab and others said: seven years. It is reported that the wife of Ibn ʿAjlan gave birth after seven years. It is reported that al-Ḍaḥḥāk ibn Muzāḥim remained in the womb for two years. He said: "I was born and my front teeth had already come out." It is reported that ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwan was born after six months.

His saying, ﴿sawāʾun minkum﴾ ("it is equal from among you"), and the rest of the verse: "sawāʾ" is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It requires after it two things that are alike. Its being in the nominative is as the predicate of the subject "man" (whoever). A verbal noun cannot be a predicate except with an implied element, as al-Khansa said:

……………………

*"Indeed she is only advance and retreat"*

meaning: possessor of advance and retreat. One group said: here the meaning is "dhū sawāʾ" (one who is equal). Al-Zajjaj said: the use of "sawāʾ" in Arabic speech became frequent until it functioned like an active participle, so it needs no implied element.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view it is like ʿadl (justice) and zūr (falsehood) and ḍayf (guest), in that they are used as descriptive nouns.

(p. 183) Another group said: the meaning is "mustawin minkum" (equal among you), so it needs no implied element. Sibawayh regarded this as weak, because it begins with an indefinite noun (nakira). The meaning of this verse: it is balanced among you in Allah's encompassment and knowledge, whether one conceals his speech so that he whispers it to himself, or speaks it aloud so that he makes it heard. Nothing is hidden from Allah, the Exalted.

His saying, ﴿wa man huwa mustakhfin bil-layl﴾ ("and whoever hides by night"), means: whoever is in the utmost concealment at night, and whoever moves about freely by day going on his way, are equal in the knowledge of Allah, blessed and exalted, and in His encompassment of both. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid took a meaning that implies: the one who hides by night and goes forth by day is one man, suspicious by night, and displaying innocence by day in his dealings with people. So this is one category, one who made the night a time of rest. The meaning: this one and the one whose whole affair is one, innocent of suspicion, are equal in Allah's awareness of all of them. This interpretation is supported by the conjunction of "sārib" without repeating "man," and its omission is not found except in poetic necessity.

"Sārib" in the language means one who acts as he wishes. Of this is the poet's saying:

*"I see every people has tied the fetter of their stallion,*
*but we have loosed its fetter, so it roams free"*

meaning: unrestrained, not turned away from any direction. This is a man who boasts of the might of his people. Of this is also the saying of another:

*"However you go, you went, though you were not one who strays,*
*and dreams bring near what is not near"*

The verse may contain three categories: one who conceals speech is one extreme, one who speaks aloud is an extreme opposite to the first, and the third is a middle one, changeable, who disobeys by night secretly and displays innocence by day. The meaning of the verse extends to deeds as well. Qutrub, as transmitted by al-Zajjaj, said: "mustakhfin" means apparent, from their saying "khafaytu al-shay'" when one reveals a thing. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"It (the rain) uncovered them from their clouds, as if*
*the rain of an evening, pouring down, had revealed them"*

He said: "sārib" means one hidden in a cave (sirb).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Although this view has a clear connection to the language, it is weak, because the pairing of night with "mustakhfin" and day with "sārib" refutes this view.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 13, verses 8–10:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying:

﴿Allah knows what every female bears, and what the wombs diminish and what they increase. And everything with Him is by measure.﴾ ﴿He is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Great, the Exalted.﴾ ﴿It is equal to Him whether one of you conceals speech or speaks aloud, and whether one hides by night or goes forth freely by day.﴾

When the disbelievers' astonishment and their denial of resurrection from the graves had preceded, Allah in these verses set forth the examples that call attention to the power of Allah, blessed and exalted, and that make resurrection possible. Among these is this one, one of the five keys to the unseen (mafatih al-ghayb). It is that Allah, blessed and exalted, alone possesses knowledge of what every female of every kind of animal carries of embryos. This beginning shows that re-creation is not difficult for the One who is capable of the first creation.

The "mā" in His saying, ﴿mā taḥmilu﴾ ("what she carries"), may be a relative pronoun (bi-ma'na alladhi) functioning as the object of "ya'lamu" (knows). It may be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), also functioning as the object of "ya'lamu." It may also be an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence, with "taḥmilu" as the predicate, though this aspect is weak. In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b (a codex attributed to a companion), the reading is: "mā taḥmilu kullu unthā wa mā taḍa'u" ("what every female carries and what she delivers").

His saying, ﴿wa mā taghīḍu al-arḥām﴾ ("and what the wombs diminish"), means: what they decrease. This derives from the meaning of ﴿wa ghīḍa al-mā'u﴾ ("and the water subsided") [Hud: 44], which is from the sense of drying up (nuḍūb). Here it means the removal and departure of something from the womb. When His saying ﴿wa mā tazdādu﴾ ("and what they increase") corresponds to it, it is interpreted as the sense of decrease. Then the commentators differed about the form of the increase and decrease. Mujahid said: The diminishing of the womb is that she sheds blood upon the pregnancy. When that happens, the child becomes weak in the womb and pale. When the pregnant woman completes nine months and does not deliver, the child remains in her womb for an additional period in which he completes from his body and health what was lost through the shedding of blood. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿wa mā taghīḍu al-arḥām wa mā tazdād﴾.

Most commentators hold that the diminishing of the womb is the release of blood upon the pregnancy. Some people held that its diminishing is the drying up of blood in it and its retention after the customary release through menstruation (ḥayḍ). Then His saying ﴿wa mā tazdād﴾ after that would run in the sense of "taghīḍ" without correspondence. Rather, the diminishing of the womb means an increase in it. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The diminishing of the womb is that the woman miscarries the child, and the increase is that she delivers him after a full term, complete in his creation. Qatada said: The diminishing is miscarriage (siqt), and the increase is that the child remains beyond nine months.

His saying, ﴿wa kullu shay'﴾ ("and everything"), is a general term covering everything to which measure applies.

Al-ghayb ("the unseen") is what is hidden from perception, and al-shahāda ("the witnessed") is what is observed among matters. He placed the verbal nouns in the place of the things, each of which must have one of the two states.

His saying "al-Kabīr" ("the Great") is an attribute of absolute magnification. "Al-Mutaʿāl" ("the Exalted") derives from ʿulūw (elevation). The readers differed about pausing (waqf) on "al-Mutaʿāl." Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr (in some of what is reported from him) pronounced the final yā' in both continuation (waṣl) and pause (waqf). The rest did not pronounce it in either continuation or pause. Its pronunciation is the normal and standard practice. Sibawayh regarded its omission at verse-endings (fawāṣil), as in this verse, as easy, by analogy with rhymes (qawāfī) in poetry. Its omission outside verse-endings or poetry is considered ugly. The reason is that since tanwīn (nunation) always replaces the definite article "al-," and this yā' is omitted along with tanwīn, it was acceptable to omit it along with what replaces it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 13, verses 11–13 (part 1 of 2)

The words of the Exalted:

﴿For each person there are successive angels, before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of Allah. Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah wills evil for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have no protector besides Him.﴾

﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, causing fear and hope, and who produces the heavy clouds.﴾

﴿The thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and the angels too, out of awe of Him. He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about Allah, while He is mighty in strength.﴾

The interpreters (al-mutawwilun) differ over the referent of the pronoun in "lahu" (for him). One group said: it refers to the name of Allah, mentioned earlier. On this view, "al-mu'aqqibat" (the successive ones) are the angels who guard the servants' deeds, and they also guard the servants themselves. This was said by al-Hasan, and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan narrated a hadith concerning it. (p-185) It is also the view of Mujahid and al-Nakha'i. On this view, the pronoun in "yadayhi" (his hands) and the pronouns after it refer to the servant mentioned in Allah's words: ﴿and one who hides himself by night﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10]. The phrase "min amri Allah" (by the command of Allah) may be an attribute of the "mu'aqqibat," or it may mean: they guard him from everything whose repelling has been decreed by destiny, and when the decreed event occurs, they leave the person to it.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: the pronoun in "lahu" refers to the one mentioned in Allah's words: ﴿and one who speaks aloud, and one who hides it﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10], and so do the rest of the pronouns in the verse. They said: on this view, "al-mu'aqqibat" are the man's guards and his enforcers who protect him. They also said: on this view, the verse concerns the disbelieving rulers. Al-Tabari chose this view, and it is the view of 'Ikrimah and a group of others. 'Ikrimah said: they are the processions before him and behind him.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On the first interpretation mentioned above, it is also valid for the pronoun in "lahu" to refer to the believing servant, meaning: Allah has appointed for him (guardians). This interpretation is, in my view, stronger, because the purpose of the verse is only to draw attention to the power of Allah. He mentioned the equality of one who hides himself and one who goes forth openly, and that for him there are successive guardians from Allah who protect him in every state. Then He mentioned that Allah does not change this state of protection for the servant until he changes what is in himself. On both interpretations, the pronouns do not refer to a specific human being.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the verse concerns the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was revealed concerning Allah's protection of him from Arbad ibn Rabi'a and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, in the story that comes later in the mention of the thunderbolts.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Although the wording of this verse fits the meaning of that story, the view is weakened by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) has not been mentioned earlier, so that the pronoun in "lahu" would refer back to him.

"Al-mu'aqqibat" are the groups in which some follow others. On the first interpretation, they are the angels, and this is in line with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Angels succeed one another among you by night and angels by day, and they gather at the Fajr and 'Asr prayers." On the second interpretation, they are the guards and attendants who belong to the kings. The word "mu'aqqibat" is the plural of "mu'aqqiba," which means a group that comes after another. The root "ta'qib" in general means that one state is followed by another state of the same kind, and sometimes by a state of a different kind. From it come "mu'aqaba" in riding (taking turns), "mu'qib" in the "uqbat al-qidr" (the turn at the cooking pot), and "mu'aqaba" in pairs. From it is the saying of Salama ibn Jandal:

"We sent the horses in their tracks, returning in succession,
with hooves worn down from the first charge to the last."

'Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad read on the pulpit: "lahu al-ma'aqib" (for him are the ma'aqib). Abu al-Fath said: it is the broken plural of "mu'qib."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is with sukun on the 'ayn and kasra on the qaf, like "mut'im" and "mata'im," and "muqdim" and "maqadim." This is the reading of Abu al-Barahsam. So it seems that "mu'qib" was pluralized as "ma'aqiba," and then the ya' in "ma'aqib" was made a substitute for the omitted ha' in "ma'aqiba." The form "mu'aqqiba" is not the plural of "mu'aqqib," as al-Tabari mentioned, comparing it to "rajul, rijal, rijalat." That is not the case, because those are like "jamal, jimal, jimalat," whereas "mu'aqqiba" and "mu'aqqibat" are like "darriba" and "darribat."

(p-187) In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "min bayni yadayhi wa raqibun min khalfihi" (from before him and a watcher from behind him). Ibn 'Abbas read: "wa raqiban min khalfihi" (and a watcher from behind him). Abu Hatim reported from him that he read: "mu'aqqibat min khalfihi wa raqibun min bayni yadayhi yahfazunahu bi-amri Allah" (successive ones from behind him and a watcher before him, guarding him by the command of Allah).

Allah's words "yahfazunahu" (they guard him) may have two meanings. One is that it means they guard him and defend him, so the pronoun is the object of the guarding. The second meaning is that it means the preservation and memorization of words, so there is then an omitted noun in the phrase, meaning: they record his deeds. This would then be of the type of: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

As for Allah's words "min amri Allah": whoever takes "yahfazunahu" to mean they guard him, then the meaning of "min amri Allah" is that the "mu'aqqibat" are intended, and so there is a transposition in the verse, meaning: for him are successive ones, from the command of Allah, who guard him before him and behind him. Abu al-Fath said: "min amri Allah" is in the nominative position because it is an attribute of a nominative noun, namely "al-mu'aqqibat." This interpretation can be combined with the first interpretation regarding "yahfazunahu." As for the one who interprets the pronoun in "lahu" as referring to the servant and makes "al-mu'aqqibat" the guards, and makes the verse about the disbelieving rulers, he takes "min amri Allah" to mean: they guard him, by their own claim, from the decree of Allah, and they repel it in their own assumption, because of their ignorance of Allah, exalted is He.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation, the one who takes it so makes them among the disbelievers. Abu al-Fath said: "min amri Allah," on this view, is in the accusative position, as in your saying: "I guarded Zayd from the lion," where "min al-asad" (from the lion) is the object of "hafiztu" (I guarded). Qatada said: the meaning of "bi-amri Allah" is that they guard him from what Allah has commanded. This is an arbitrary interpretation. Others said: the meaning is protection from the command of Allah, and something similar to this was mentioned before. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them, read: "yahfazunahu bi-amri Allah."

(p-188) Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that He does not change the condition of a people by punishing them and testing them with retribution, until they themselves commit acts of disobedience and change what they were commanded regarding obedience to Allah. This is a point requiring reflection, because it introduces into this statement what the Shari'a has established regarding the general body being taken to account for the sins of the elite. Among this is Allah's saying: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have wronged﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. Among this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), when it was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be destroyed while righteous people are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness becomes widespread." And there are many other things like this. So Allah's words "hatta yughayyiru" (until they change) mean: until a change takes place, either from them, or from the one who observes them, or from one who is among them by way of causation. Just as Allah changed the condition of those who fled at the Battle of Uhud because of the archers changing what was in themselves, and other examples from the Shari'a. So the meaning of the verse is not that no punishment descends upon anyone except when he has previously committed a sin. Rather, calamities may descend due to the sins of others, and there are also calamities that Allah intends for the reward of the one afflicted, and those are not a change (of condition).

Then, blessed and exalted is He, informed that when Allah wills evil for a people, there is no repelling it and no protection from it. This was placed in the context of drawing attention to the custom of Allah, exalted is He, and His power. Good and evil are on the same level: when Allah wills either of them for a servant, it is not turned back. However, He singled out evil for mention so that the verse would contain a warning.

The readers differed over "wali" (protector). Some of them inclined the alif (imala), and some did not. The "wali" is the one who takes charge of a person's affairs, like "waliyy." Both come from wilaya (guardianship), like "'alim" and "'alim" from 'ilm (knowledge).

Allah's words: ﴿It is He who shows you﴾ and the rest of the verse. This is a verse drawing attention to power. Concerning "al-barq" (lightning), it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it is a whip in the hand of an angel with which he drives the clouds. This is the most authentic thing narrated about it. (p-189) It is also narrated from some scholars that they said: lightning is the collision of bodies. In my view this is rejected. Abu al-Jald said concerning this verse: "al-barq" is water. Makki mentioned this from Ibn 'Abbas. The meaning of this statement is that, since lightning is the herald of water, and since travelers fear water and the resident hopes for it, he expressed it by the term water.

As for Allah's words: ﴿causing fear and hope﴾, whoever says this refers to water, the meaning is as previously explained. The apparent meaning is that the fear is from the thunderbolts of lightning, and the hope is for the rain that comes with it, and this is the view of al-Hasan. "Al-sahab" (clouds) is the plural of "sahaba," and the plural of the attribute is the same. "Al-thiqal" (heavy) means carrying water, and this is how Qatada and Mujahid explained it. The Arabs describe clouds this way, and from it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"No garden among the gardens of the sand-grouse
is more beautiful than it, nor a cloud
heavy with water, whose downpour is unveiled."

"Al-daluh" means the heavily laden one.

(p-190) "Al-Ra'd" (thunder) is an angel who drives the clouds with his voice, and this audible voice of his is a glorification. "Al-Ra'd" is also the name of the angel, and it has been said: "al-ra'd" is the name of the angel's voice. It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he heard thunder he would say: "O Allah, do not destroy us with Your anger, do not kill us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that."

It was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and others, that when they heard thunder they would say: "Glory be to the One whom You glorify." It was narrated from Abu Hurayra that "the Prophet (ﷺ) when he heard thunder said: 'Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise.'" Ibn Abi Zakariyya said: "Whoever says when he hears thunder, 'Glory be to Allah and with His praise,' a thunderbolt will not strike him." It has also been said concerning thunder that it is a wind that is choked between the clouds. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view there is something to examine in this, because these are the opinions of the naturalists and others among the heretics. It was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when the angel becomes angry and drives the clouds, they tremble out of fear of him, and so lightning occurs, and when they rub against each other, thunderbolts occur.

Allah's words: ﴿and He sends the thunderbolts﴾ and the rest of the verse. It has been said that He included this in the drawing of attention to power without a cause that prompted it. Ibn Jurayj said: the cause of its revelation was the story of Arbad, brother of Labid ibn Rabi'a through their mother, and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl. Concerning the matter of the two of them, it is narrated that "they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him to make the affair after him pass to 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, and that they would enter his religion. He refused. 'Amir said: 'Then you will be over the people of the cities and I over the people of the desert.' He refused. 'Amir said to him: 'Then what will you give me?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'I will give you the reins of the horses, for you are a brave horseman.' 'Amir said to him: 'By Allah, I will fill it over you with horses and men until I take you.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Allah refuses that, and so do the sons of Qayla.' The two of them left (p-191) from his presence, and one of them said to his companion: 'If we had killed him, not two goats would butt heads over him.' So they conspired to return for that. 'Amir said to Arbad: 'I will occupy him for you with conversation, and you strike him with the sword.' 'Amir kept talking to him while Arbad did nothing. When they departed, 'Amir said to him: 'By Allah, O Arbad, I will never fear you again, though I used to fear you before this.' Arbad said to him: 'By Allah, I did intend to draw the sword, but I could not do it. I kept seeing you between me and him. Shall I strike you?' Then they went to the gathering before the Prophet (ﷺ), and a thunderbolt struck Arbad and killed him." Concerning this, his brother Labid ibn Rabi'a says:

"I fear for Arbad the calamities of death,
yet I do not dread the rising of the Pleiades or the Lions,
The thunder and the thunderbolts have bereaved me
of the horseman, on the day of the terrible battle, the brave one."

And the verse was revealed concerning that. It is also related from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ṣuḥār al-ʿAbdī that it reached him that a tyrant among the tyrants of the Arabs had been sent for by the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he might embrace Islam. He said: "Tell me about the God of Muḥammad: is He made of pearl or of gold?" Then a thunderbolt struck him, and the verse was revealed concerning him. His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they dispute about God﴾. It may be that this refers to the dispute of the aforementioned Jew, with the wāw being the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl). Generous in gift, mighty in power (shadīd al-mihāl).

Let not their cross prevail,
Nor their scheming against your scheming (mihālaka).
