Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 13, verses 11–13 (part 1 of 2)

The words of the Exalted:

﴿For each person there are successive angels, before him and behind him, who guard him by the command of Allah. Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah wills evil for a people, there is no repelling it, and they have no protector besides Him.﴾

﴿It is He who shows you the lightning, causing fear and hope, and who produces the heavy clouds.﴾

﴿The thunder glorifies Him with His praise, and the angels too, out of awe of Him. He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, yet they dispute about Allah, while He is mighty in strength.﴾

The interpreters (al-mutawwilun) differ over the referent of the pronoun in "lahu" (for him). One group said: it refers to the name of Allah, mentioned earlier. On this view, "al-mu'aqqibat" (the successive ones) are the angels who guard the servants' deeds, and they also guard the servants themselves. This was said by al-Hasan, and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan narrated a hadith concerning it. (p-185) It is also the view of Mujahid and al-Nakha'i. On this view, the pronoun in "yadayhi" (his hands) and the pronouns after it refer to the servant mentioned in Allah's words: ﴿and one who hides himself by night﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10]. The phrase "min amri Allah" (by the command of Allah) may be an attribute of the "mu'aqqibat," or it may mean: they guard him from everything whose repelling has been decreed by destiny, and when the decreed event occurs, they leave the person to it.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: the pronoun in "lahu" refers to the one mentioned in Allah's words: ﴿and one who speaks aloud, and one who hides it﴾ [al-Ra'd: 10], and so do the rest of the pronouns in the verse. They said: on this view, "al-mu'aqqibat" are the man's guards and his enforcers who protect him. They also said: on this view, the verse concerns the disbelieving rulers. Al-Tabari chose this view, and it is the view of 'Ikrimah and a group of others. 'Ikrimah said: they are the processions before him and behind him.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On the first interpretation mentioned above, it is also valid for the pronoun in "lahu" to refer to the believing servant, meaning: Allah has appointed for him (guardians). This interpretation is, in my view, stronger, because the purpose of the verse is only to draw attention to the power of Allah. He mentioned the equality of one who hides himself and one who goes forth openly, and that for him there are successive guardians from Allah who protect him in every state. Then He mentioned that Allah does not change this state of protection for the servant until he changes what is in himself. On both interpretations, the pronouns do not refer to a specific human being.

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: the verse concerns the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was revealed concerning Allah's protection of him from Arbad ibn Rabi'a and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, in the story that comes later in the mention of the thunderbolts.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Although the wording of this verse fits the meaning of that story, the view is weakened by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) has not been mentioned earlier, so that the pronoun in "lahu" would refer back to him.

"Al-mu'aqqibat" are the groups in which some follow others. On the first interpretation, they are the angels, and this is in line with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Angels succeed one another among you by night and angels by day, and they gather at the Fajr and 'Asr prayers." On the second interpretation, they are the guards and attendants who belong to the kings. The word "mu'aqqibat" is the plural of "mu'aqqiba," which means a group that comes after another. The root "ta'qib" in general means that one state is followed by another state of the same kind, and sometimes by a state of a different kind. From it come "mu'aqaba" in riding (taking turns), "mu'qib" in the "uqbat al-qidr" (the turn at the cooking pot), and "mu'aqaba" in pairs. From it is the saying of Salama ibn Jandal:

"We sent the horses in their tracks, returning in succession,
with hooves worn down from the first charge to the last."

'Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad read on the pulpit: "lahu al-ma'aqib" (for him are the ma'aqib). Abu al-Fath said: it is the broken plural of "mu'qib."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is with sukun on the 'ayn and kasra on the qaf, like "mut'im" and "mata'im," and "muqdim" and "maqadim." This is the reading of Abu al-Barahsam. So it seems that "mu'qib" was pluralized as "ma'aqiba," and then the ya' in "ma'aqib" was made a substitute for the omitted ha' in "ma'aqiba." The form "mu'aqqiba" is not the plural of "mu'aqqib," as al-Tabari mentioned, comparing it to "rajul, rijal, rijalat." That is not the case, because those are like "jamal, jimal, jimalat," whereas "mu'aqqiba" and "mu'aqqibat" are like "darriba" and "darribat."

(p-187) In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "min bayni yadayhi wa raqibun min khalfihi" (from before him and a watcher from behind him). Ibn 'Abbas read: "wa raqiban min khalfihi" (and a watcher from behind him). Abu Hatim reported from him that he read: "mu'aqqibat min khalfihi wa raqibun min bayni yadayhi yahfazunahu bi-amri Allah" (successive ones from behind him and a watcher before him, guarding him by the command of Allah).

Allah's words "yahfazunahu" (they guard him) may have two meanings. One is that it means they guard him and defend him, so the pronoun is the object of the guarding. The second meaning is that it means the preservation and memorization of words, so there is then an omitted noun in the phrase, meaning: they record his deeds. This would then be of the type of: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

As for Allah's words "min amri Allah": whoever takes "yahfazunahu" to mean they guard him, then the meaning of "min amri Allah" is that the "mu'aqqibat" are intended, and so there is a transposition in the verse, meaning: for him are successive ones, from the command of Allah, who guard him before him and behind him. Abu al-Fath said: "min amri Allah" is in the nominative position because it is an attribute of a nominative noun, namely "al-mu'aqqibat." This interpretation can be combined with the first interpretation regarding "yahfazunahu." As for the one who interprets the pronoun in "lahu" as referring to the servant and makes "al-mu'aqqibat" the guards, and makes the verse about the disbelieving rulers, he takes "min amri Allah" to mean: they guard him, by their own claim, from the decree of Allah, and they repel it in their own assumption, because of their ignorance of Allah, exalted is He.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this interpretation, the one who takes it so makes them among the disbelievers. Abu al-Fath said: "min amri Allah," on this view, is in the accusative position, as in your saying: "I guarded Zayd from the lion," where "min al-asad" (from the lion) is the object of "hafiztu" (I guarded). Qatada said: the meaning of "bi-amri Allah" is that they guard him from what Allah has commanded. This is an arbitrary interpretation. Others said: the meaning is protection from the command of Allah, and something similar to this was mentioned before. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad, may Allah be pleased with them, read: "yahfazunahu bi-amri Allah."

(p-188) Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that He does not change the condition of a people by punishing them and testing them with retribution, until they themselves commit acts of disobedience and change what they were commanded regarding obedience to Allah. This is a point requiring reflection, because it introduces into this statement what the Shari'a has established regarding the general body being taken to account for the sins of the elite. Among this is Allah's saying: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have wronged﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. Among this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), when it was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be destroyed while righteous people are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness becomes widespread." And there are many other things like this. So Allah's words "hatta yughayyiru" (until they change) mean: until a change takes place, either from them, or from the one who observes them, or from one who is among them by way of causation. Just as Allah changed the condition of those who fled at the Battle of Uhud because of the archers changing what was in themselves, and other examples from the Shari'a. So the meaning of the verse is not that no punishment descends upon anyone except when he has previously committed a sin. Rather, calamities may descend due to the sins of others, and there are also calamities that Allah intends for the reward of the one afflicted, and those are not a change (of condition).

Then, blessed and exalted is He, informed that when Allah wills evil for a people, there is no repelling it and no protection from it. This was placed in the context of drawing attention to the custom of Allah, exalted is He, and His power. Good and evil are on the same level: when Allah wills either of them for a servant, it is not turned back. However, He singled out evil for mention so that the verse would contain a warning.

The readers differed over "wali" (protector). Some of them inclined the alif (imala), and some did not. The "wali" is the one who takes charge of a person's affairs, like "waliyy." Both come from wilaya (guardianship), like "'alim" and "'alim" from 'ilm (knowledge).

Allah's words: ﴿It is He who shows you﴾ and the rest of the verse. This is a verse drawing attention to power. Concerning "al-barq" (lightning), it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it is a whip in the hand of an angel with which he drives the clouds. This is the most authentic thing narrated about it. (p-189) It is also narrated from some scholars that they said: lightning is the collision of bodies. In my view this is rejected. Abu al-Jald said concerning this verse: "al-barq" is water. Makki mentioned this from Ibn 'Abbas. The meaning of this statement is that, since lightning is the herald of water, and since travelers fear water and the resident hopes for it, he expressed it by the term water.

As for Allah's words: ﴿causing fear and hope﴾, whoever says this refers to water, the meaning is as previously explained. The apparent meaning is that the fear is from the thunderbolts of lightning, and the hope is for the rain that comes with it, and this is the view of al-Hasan. "Al-sahab" (clouds) is the plural of "sahaba," and the plural of the attribute is the same. "Al-thiqal" (heavy) means carrying water, and this is how Qatada and Mujahid explained it. The Arabs describe clouds this way, and from it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"No garden among the gardens of the sand-grouse
is more beautiful than it, nor a cloud
heavy with water, whose downpour is unveiled."

"Al-daluh" means the heavily laden one.

(p-190) "Al-Ra'd" (thunder) is an angel who drives the clouds with his voice, and this audible voice of his is a glorification. "Al-Ra'd" is also the name of the angel, and it has been said: "al-ra'd" is the name of the angel's voice. It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he heard thunder he would say: "O Allah, do not destroy us with Your anger, do not kill us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that."

It was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and others, that when they heard thunder they would say: "Glory be to the One whom You glorify." It was narrated from Abu Hurayra that "the Prophet (ﷺ) when he heard thunder said: 'Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise.'" Ibn Abi Zakariyya said: "Whoever says when he hears thunder, 'Glory be to Allah and with His praise,' a thunderbolt will not strike him." It has also been said concerning thunder that it is a wind that is choked between the clouds. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view there is something to examine in this, because these are the opinions of the naturalists and others among the heretics. It was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when the angel becomes angry and drives the clouds, they tremble out of fear of him, and so lightning occurs, and when they rub against each other, thunderbolts occur.

Allah's words: ﴿and He sends the thunderbolts﴾ and the rest of the verse. It has been said that He included this in the drawing of attention to power without a cause that prompted it. The thunder and the thunderbolts have bereaved me

And the verse was revealed concerning that. (p-188) Then Allah, exalted is He, informed that He does not change the condition of a people by punishing them and testing them with retribution, until they themselves commit acts of disobedience and change what they were commanded regarding obedience to Allah. Among this is Allah's saying: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have wronged﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. Among this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), when it was said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, will we be destroyed while righteous people are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness becomes widespread." And there are many other things like this. So Allah's words "hatta yughayyiru" (until they change) mean: until a change takes place, either from them, or from the one who observes them, or from one who is among them by way of causation. Just as Allah changed the condition of those who fled at the Battle of Uhud because of the archers changing what was in themselves, and other examples from the Shari'a. So the meaning of the verse is not that no punishment descends upon anyone except when he has previously committed a sin. Rather, calamities may descend due to the sins of others, and there are also calamities that Allah intends for the reward of the one afflicted, and those are not a change (of condition).

Then, blessed and exalted is He, informed that when Allah wills evil for a people, there is no repelling it and no protection from it. This was placed in the context of drawing attention to the custom of Allah, exalted is He, and His power. Good and evil are on the same level: when Allah wills either of them for a servant, it is not turned back. However, He singled out evil for mention so that the verse would contain a warning.

The readers differed over "wali" (protector). Some of them inclined the alif (imala), and some did not. The "wali" is the one who takes charge of a person's affairs, like "waliyy." Both come from wilaya (guardianship), like "'alim" and "'alim" from 'ilm (knowledge).

Allah's words: ﴿It is He who shows you﴾ and the rest of the verse. This is a verse drawing attention to power. Concerning "al-barq" (lightning), it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it is a whip in the hand of an angel with which he drives the clouds. This is the most authentic thing narrated about it. (p-189) It is also narrated from some scholars that they said: lightning is the collision of bodies. In my view this is rejected. Abu al-Jald said concerning this verse: "al-barq" is water. Makki mentioned this from Ibn 'Abbas. The meaning of this statement is that, since lightning is the herald of water, and since travelers fear water and the resident hopes for it, he expressed it by the term water.

As for Allah's words: ﴿causing fear and hope﴾, whoever says this refers to water, the meaning is as previously explained. The apparent meaning is that the fear is from the thunderbolts of lightning, and the hope is for the rain that comes with it, and this is the view of al-Hasan. "Al-sahab" (clouds) is the plural of "sahaba," and the plural of the attribute is the same. "Al-thiqal" (heavy) means carrying water, and this is how Qatada and Mujahid explained it. The Arabs describe clouds this way, and from it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"No garden among the gardens of the sand-grouse
is more beautiful than it, nor a cloud
heavy with water, whose downpour is unveiled."

"Al-daluh" means the heavily laden one.

(p-190) "Al-Ra'd" (thunder) is an angel who drives the clouds with his voice, and this audible voice of his is a glorification. "Al-Ra'd" is also the name of the angel, and it has been said: "al-ra'd" is the name of the angel's voice. It was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he heard thunder he would say: "O Allah, do not destroy us with Your anger, do not kill us with Your punishment, and grant us well-being before that."

It was narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and others, that when they heard thunder they would say: "Glory be to the One whom You glorify." It was narrated from Abu Hurayra that "the Prophet (ﷺ) when he heard thunder said: 'Glory be to Him whom the thunder glorifies with His praise.'" Ibn Abi Zakariyya said: "Whoever says when he hears thunder, 'Glory be to Allah and with His praise,' a thunderbolt will not strike him." It has also been said concerning thunder that it is a wind that is choked between the clouds. This was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view there is something to examine in this, because these are the opinions of the naturalists and others among the heretics. It was also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when the angel becomes angry and drives the clouds, they tremble out of fear of him, and so lightning occurs, and when they rub against each other, thunderbolts occur.

Allah's words: ﴿and He sends the thunderbolts﴾ and the rest of the verse. It has been said that He included this in the drawing of attention to power without a cause that prompted it. Ibn Jurayj said: the cause of its revelation was the story of Arbad, brother of Labid ibn Rabi'a through their mother, and 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl. Concerning the matter of the two of them, it is narrated that "they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him to make the affair after him pass to 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, and that they would enter his religion. He refused. 'Amir said: 'Then you will be over the people of the cities and I over the people of the desert.' He refused. 'Amir said to him: 'Then what will you give me?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'I will give you the reins of the horses, for you are a brave horseman.' 'Amir said to him: 'By Allah, I will fill it over you with horses and men until I take you.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Allah refuses that, and so do the sons of Qayla.' The two of them left (p-191) from his presence, and one of them said to his companion: 'If we had killed him, not two goats would butt heads over him.' So they conspired to return for that. 'Amir said to Arbad: 'I will occupy him for you with conversation, and you strike him with the sword.' 'Amir kept talking to him while Arbad did nothing. When they departed, 'Amir said to him: 'By Allah, O Arbad, I will never fear you again, though I used to fear you before this.' Arbad said to him: 'By Allah, I did intend to draw the sword, but I could not do it. I kept seeing you between me and him. Shall I strike you?' Then they went to the gathering before the Prophet (ﷺ), and a thunderbolt struck Arbad and killed him." Concerning this, his brother Labid ibn Rabi'a says:

"I fear for Arbad the calamities of death,
yet I do not dread the rising of the Pleiades or the Lions,
The thunder and the thunderbolts have bereaved me
of the horseman, on the day of the terrible battle, the brave one."

And the verse was revealed concerning that. It is also related from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Ṣuḥār al-ʿAbdī that it reached him that a tyrant among the tyrants of the Arabs had been sent for by the Prophet (ﷺ) so that he might embrace Islam. He said: "Tell me about the God of Muḥammad: is He made of pearl or of gold?" Then a thunderbolt struck him, and the verse was revealed concerning him. Mujāhid said: Some Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) to dispute with him, and while they were in that state, a thunderbolt descended and seized the top of his skull, and the verse was revealed concerning him.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they dispute about God﴾. It may be that this refers to the dispute of the aforementioned Jew, with the wāw being the wāw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl). Or it may refer to the dispute of the aforementioned tyrant. It is also permissible, if the verse was not revealed on a specific occasion, that His words ﴿And they dispute about God﴾ refer to all the disbelievers among the Arabs and others to whom these warnings were addressed.

Al-mihāl means power and destruction, and from it is the verse of al-Aʿshā:

A shoot of the nabʿ tree, swaying on the branch of glory,
Generous in gift, mighty in power (shadīd al-mihāl).

From it is also the verse of ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib:

Let not their cross prevail,
Nor their scheming against your scheming (mihālaka).

Al-Aʿraj and al-Ḍaḥḥāk recited "al-maḥāl" with a fatḥah on the mīm, meaning "al-maḥālah," which is stratagem (al-ḥīlah). From it is the Arab saying concerning the proverb: "A man is honoured, without doubt (lā maḥālah)." This is like the idea of gradual seizure (istidrāj), deceit, and the like. These are metaphors (istiʿārāt) used in speaking of God, exalted is He. When the mīm is kasrah it is original (ṣalliyyah), and when it is fatḥah it is an added letter (zāʾidah). It is said: "Maḥala al-rajulu bi al-rajul," when he schemes against him and seizes him with severe contrivance.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 13, verses 14–16:

﴿To Him is the true supplication. Those whom they invoke besides Him do not respond to them with anything, except like one who stretches his hands out toward water so that it may reach his mouth, but it will never reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ ﴿To Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and unwillingly, and their shadows at the mornings and evenings.﴾ ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?" Say: "Allah." Say: "Have you then taken besides Him protectors who do not possess for themselves any benefit or harm?" Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal? Or are the darknesses and the light equal? Or have they attributed to Allah partners who create as He creates, so that the creation seems alike to them?" Say: "Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Subduer."﴾

The pronoun in "lahu" (to Him) refers to the name of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted. Ibn 'Abbas said: "﴿The true supplication﴾ is: there is no god but Allah," and whatever is of the Sharia (divine law) in its meaning. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is the Tawhid" (affirmation of God's oneness). It is also valid that its meaning is: to Him is the supplication of the servants in truth, while the invocation of others, the idols, is false.

His words "those whom" refer to what is worshipped besides Allah. The pronoun in "yad'una" (they invoke) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and those like them among the Arabs. Al-Yazidi related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' the reading "tad'una min dunihi" with the "ta" at the top (i.e., the second-person form). "Yastajibuna" means "yujibuna" (they respond). From this is the words of the poet:

"A caller called: O you who answers the call to generosity, *** but no answerer answered him at that time."

The meaning of the statement is: those whom the disbelievers invoke for their needs and their benefits do not respond to them with anything.

Then the Exalted gave an example of their responses: one who stretches his hands toward water and gestures to it to come to his mouth, but it never reaches his mouth. Likewise, the response of these (idols) and benefit from them never occurs. His words "huwa" (it) refer to the water, and the one who reaches it is the water. The pronoun in "bali'ihi" (reaching it) refers to the mouth. It is also valid that "huwa" refers to the mouth, which is the one reaching, and the pronoun in "bali'ihi" refers to the water, because the mouth never reaches the water in that state. Then the Exalted informed about the supplication of the disbelievers that it is in error, in which nothing benefits and nothing avails.

His Exalted words: ﴿To Allah prostrates﴾ (the verse). The apparent wording of these expressions may imply that it is said as an admonition of Allah's power and the subjugation of things to Him only. It may also imply a rebuke of the disbelievers of Quraysh and those present with Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning: if you yourselves do not believe with certainty and do not prostrate, then all who are in the heavens and the earth prostrate to Allah, the Exalted. To this interpretation al-Tabari inclined. "Man" (whoever) applies generally to the angels, and their prostration is willing without any disagreement. As for the people of the earth, the believers among them are included in "man," and their prostration is willing. As for the prostration of the disbelievers, it is unwilling. This is in two ways according to this meaning: if we take prostration to be this known bodily posture, then what is meant by the disbelievers is those whom the sword compels to Islam, as Qatada said, so they prostrate unwillingly, either out of hypocrisy, or the unwillingness is at the beginning of their state, and this attribute persists upon them even if their faith is later sound. And if we take prostration to mean submission and humbling, according to what it means in the language, as in the words of the poet:

"..............................  *** you see the hills in it prostrating to the hooves."

Then all disbelievers enter into "man," because there is no disbeliever except that he is subjected, by the power of Allah, to kinds of humbling and submission more than can be counted, according to his afflictions and considerations. Al-Nahhas and al-Zajjaj said that unwillingness occurs in the prostration of disobedient Muslims and those among them who are lazy.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"Even if the wording implies this, it is unsound in terms of the intended meaning of the verse."

His Exalted words: ﴿and their shadows at the mornings and evenings﴾ is an information that the "shadows" have a prostration to Allah, the Exalted, at dawn and in the evenings. Al-Tabari said: this is like His Exalted words: ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline to the right and to the left, prostrating to Allah?﴾ [al-Nahl: 48]. He said: that is its shade in the evening. Mujahid said: "The shadow of the disbeliever prostrates willingly while he is unwilling." Ibn 'Abbas said: "The shadow of the disbeliever prostrates when it turns from his right and left." Al-Zajjaj related that some people said that "shadows" here means the persons themselves, and Abu Ishaq considered this weak. "Al-asal" is the plural of "asil" (evening). Abu Mijlaz read "wal-iysal," and Abu al-Fath said it is the verbal noun of "asalna," meaning we entered the evening, like "asbahna" (we entered the morning) and "amsayna" (we entered the evening). It is related that when the disbeliever prostrates to his idol, his shadow then prostrates to Allah, the Exalted.

His Exalted words: ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?"﴾ (the verse). The question and answer in this verse came from one direction, since the question and the affirmation concerned a matter that is clear, which no one disputes, one committed to the proof. So hastening to the answer was more eloquent in argumentation and swifter in silencing them than waiting for their answer, since there is no answer except this one, to which they hastened. Makki said: they did not know the answer and sought it from the questioner, so the questioner informed them of it. When it was established from all this that Allah, the Exalted, is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the rebuke came for taking protectors besides Him who are described as not benefiting themselves nor harming them, and this is the utmost of incapacity. Within this statement is: "You abandoned Him, while He is the One in whose hand is the dominion of all things," and the phrase ﴿besides Him﴾ implies that.

Then, after this, He depicted the disbelievers and the believers with His words: ﴿Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal?"﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "tastawi al-zulumatu" with the "ta." Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "yastawi" with the "ya." The feminine form is better, because the noun is feminine and is not separated from its verb by anything, while the masculine is common, because the feminine here is not real and the verb is placed first. This verse likened the disbeliever to the blind and disbelief to darknesses, and likened the believer to the seeing and faith to light. Then He questioned them further, whether they had seen any creation other than Allah's, which led them to the confusion between it and what Allah created, so that they made a god other than Allah. Then He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ), upon whom be blessings and peace, to declare plainly the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, that He is the Creator of all things. This is a general term in its wording, intended as particular in everything that is the creation of Allah, the Exalted. Excluded from this are the attributes of His essence, for there is no lord other than Him, and the Qur'an. He described Himself with oneness, in that there is no existent except by Him, and He, in His existence, is independent of the existents. There is no god but Him, the Most High, the Most Great.

His Exalted words: ﴿and their shadows at the mornings and evenings﴾ is an information that the "shadows" have a prostration to Allah, the Exalted, at dawn and in the evenings. Al-Tabari said: this is like His Exalted words: ﴿Have they not seen what things Allah has created, whose shadows incline to the right and to the left, prostrating to Allah?﴾ [al-Nahl: 48]. He said: that is its shade in the evening. Mujahid said: "The shadow of the disbeliever prostrates willingly while he is unwilling." Ibn 'Abbas said: "The shadow of the disbeliever prostrates when it turns from his right and left." Al-Zajjaj related that some people said that "shadows" here means the persons themselves, and Abu Ishaq considered this weak. "Al-asal" is the plural of "asil" (evening). Abu Mijlaz read "wal-iysal," and Abu al-Fath said it is the verbal noun of "asalna," meaning we entered the evening, like "asbahna" (we entered the morning) and "amsayna" (we entered the evening). It is related that when the disbeliever prostrates to his idol, his shadow then prostrates to Allah, the Exalted.

His Exalted words: ﴿Say: "Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?"﴾ (the verse). The question and answer in this verse came from one direction, since the question and the affirmation concerned a matter that is clear, which no one disputes, one committed to the proof. So hastening to the answer was more eloquent in argumentation and swifter in silencing them than waiting for their answer, since there is no answer except this one, to which they hastened. Makki said: they did not know the answer and sought it from the questioner, so the questioner informed them of it. When it was established from all this that Allah, the Exalted, is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, the rebuke came for taking protectors besides Him who are described as not benefiting themselves nor harming them, and this is the utmost of incapacity. Within this statement is: "You abandoned Him, while He is the One in whose hand is the dominion of all things," and the phrase ﴿besides Him﴾ implies that.

Then, after this, He depicted the disbelievers and the believers with His words: ﴿Say: "Are the blind and the seeing equal?"﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim read "tastawi al-zulumatu" with the "ta." Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "yastawi" with the "ya." The feminine form is better, because the noun is feminine and is not separated from its verb by anything, while the masculine is common, because the feminine here is not real and the verb is placed first. This verse likened the disbeliever to the blind and disbelief to darknesses, and likened the believer to the seeing and faith to light. Then He questioned them further, whether they had seen any creation other than Allah's, which led them to the confusion between it and what Allah created, so that they made a god other than Allah. Then He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ), upon whom be blessings and peace, to declare plainly the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, that He is the Creator of all things. This is a general term in its wording, intended as particular in everything that is the creation of Allah, the Exalted. Excluded from this are the attributes of His essence, for there is no lord other than Him, and the Qur'an. He described Himself with oneness, in that there is no existent except by Him, and He, in His existence, is independent of the existents. There is no god but Him, the Most High, the Most Great.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 13, verse 17:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿He sends down water from the sky, and the valleys flow according to their measure, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from that which they heat in the fire, seeking an ornament or goods, there is a foam like it. Thus does Allah strike the parable of truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it passes away as scum; but that which benefits mankind remains on the earth. Thus does Allah strike the parables.﴾

The beginning of this verse is an admonition regarding the power of Allah, and an establishment of proof against the disbelievers in Him. Then, when He finished mentioning that, He made it an example of truth and falsehood, and of faith and disbelief, and of doubt in the Law and certainty regarding it.

"Water" (māʾ): He means by it the rain. "The valleys" (al-awdiya): the low-lying areas and ditches between the mountains. His saying, Glorified is He, "according to their measure" (bi-qadariha) may mean according to what He has decreed for them of water, and it may mean according to the amount they can carry, in accordance with their smallness and largeness. The majority of people recited "bi-qadariha" with a fatha on the dal, while al-Ashhab al-ʿUqaylī recited it with a sukun on it.

"Foam" (zabad): what the torrent carries of debris and the like, and what it casts out from its two banks of bubbling froth. From it is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

The sea, when the northern wind blows,
is falsehood, and it casts up the flotsam with its foam.

"Rābī" (swelling): that which has swelled up and risen, and from it comes "rabwa" (a raised height).

His saying, Exalted is He, "wa-mimmā" (and from that which) is the predicate of an inchoative, the inchoative being His saying "zabadun" (foam), and "mithlahu" (like it) is an epithet for "zabad". The meaning: and from among the things which you kindle the fire upon, seeking ornaments, which are gold and silver, and seeking enjoyment of what is in utensils, which are iron, lead, copper and the like of things upon which you kindle the fire. He, Exalted is He, informs that from these also, when heated upon them, there comes a foam similar to the foam which the torrent carries. Then He struck this as a parable of truth and falsehood, meaning that the water which the earth drinks, so that benefit comes through it, is like truth, and the foam which dries up, scatters and goes away is like falsehood. Likewise, what is purified of gold, silver, iron and the like is like truth, and what goes off into the smoke is like falsehood. His saying "fī al-nār" (in the fire) is attached to an elided element whose estimate is: being such-and-such. Makkī and others said: they prevented it from being attached to His saying "yūqidūna" (they kindle), because they claimed that nothing is kindled upon except that it is in the fire; and attaching the preposition to "yūqidūna" entails specifying one state from another state. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī went to its being attached to "yūqidūna", and said: it may be kindled upon something that is not in the fire, like His saying: ﴿So kindle for me, O Hāmān, upon the clay﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 38]. That structure which he was commanded to build was kindled upon, yet it was not in the fire, but its flame reached it.

His saying "jufāʾan" (as scum) is a verbal noun from your saying "jafaʾat al-qidr" (the cooking pot foamed over) when it boiled until its foam came out and departed. Ruʾba recited "jufālan", from their saying "jafalat al-rīḥ al-saḥāb" (the wind scattered the clouds) when it carried them and dispersed them. Abū Ḥātim said: the recitation of the Bedouins is not taken into account in the Qur'an.

His saying "mā yanfaʿu al-nās" (that which benefits mankind) means the pure part of the water and of those ores. Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim in the narration of Abū Bakr, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj, Shayba and al-Ḥasan recited "tūqidūna" with the taʾ, meaning: you, O kindlers, and it is a description of all types of people. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Mujāhid, Ṭalḥa, Yaḥyā and the people of Kufa recited "yūqidūna" with the yāʾ, referring to the people. "Jufāʾan" is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: His saying, "min al-samāʾ" (from the sky), means by it the Law and the religion. His saying "fasālat awdiyatun" (the valleys flowed) means by it the hearts, meaning: the noble takes his share and the dull takes his share.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a saying that is not sound from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Allah knows best, for it tends toward the sayings of the people of symbols, and al-Ghazālī and the people of that path have relied upon it; and there is no basis for removing the expression from the understanding of Arabic speech without a cause that calls for it. Allah is the one who grants success to what is right, by His mercy. And if this saying is sound from Ibn ʿAbbās, then he only intended that His saying, "Thus does Allah strike the parable of truth and falsehood," means: the truth that is established in the hearts, and falsehood: that which afflicts them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 13, verses 18–21:

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿For those who answered their Lord is the best [reward]. And those who did not answer Him—even if they had all that is on the earth and the like of it with it, they would surely ransom themselves with it. Those will have the worst reckoning, and their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.﴾ ﴿Is the one who knows that what has been sent down to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only people of understanding are mindful.﴾ ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of God and do not break the pact,﴾ ﴿and those who join what God has commanded to be joined, and fear their Lord and dread the worst reckoning.﴾

﴿Those who answered﴾ [Al 'Imran: 172] are the believers whom God called, through the tongue of His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), and they responded to him by following the religion to which he called them.

"Al-husna" (the best [reward]) is Paradise. This includes victory in this world and similar good tidings that come to the believer, and everything that is specific to the believers of the blessings of God, the Mighty and Majestic.

﴿Those who did not answer﴾ are the disbelievers. "Su' al-hisab" (the worst reckoning) is to be scrutinised strictly by the one who reckons, and that no excess be overlooked in their account. This was said by Hawshab, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, Farqad al-Sabkhi and others. "Al-ma'wa" is the place where a person takes refuge and dwells, and "al-mihad" is that which is spread out and used for sitting and sleeping.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is the one who knows﴾ is an interrogative in the sense of affirmation. The meaning is: Are equal the one whom God has guided, so that he believed in you and knew the truth of your prophethood, and the one who was not guided and was not granted insight, so he remained in his disbelief? God, the Mighty and Majestic, illustrated this with blindness. It is related that this verse was revealed concerning Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib and Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. It was also said that it was revealed concerning 'Ammar ibn Yasir and Abu Jahl. Beyond this, it is an example applying to the whole world. "Innama" in this verse is restrictive, meaning: only the one who has intellect and understanding is mindful, so that he believes and is watchful of God.

Then, blessed and exalted is He, began describing those whom He facilitated for faith, saying: ﴿Those who fulfil the covenant of God﴾. His saying ﴿the covenant of God﴾ is a generic noun, meaning all His covenants, which are His commands and prohibitions that He enjoined upon His servants. These words include adherence to all obligations and avoidance of all sins.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not break the pact﴾ may mean by it the category of pacts, that is, when they make a covenant in obedience to God, they do not break it. Qatada said: God has laid down to His servants the prohibition against breaking the pact in some twenty verses. It may also refer to a specific pact, which is the one God took from His servants at the time He wiped over the back of their father Adam (peace be upon him).

Joining what God commanded to be joined: its apparent meaning concerns kinship ties, but it also encompasses all acts of obedience. "Su' al-hisab" is to be scrutinised strictly, with no leniency or pardon in it.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya on verses 22–24 of Sūrat al-Raʿd:

God Almighty says:

﴿Those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord, establish the prayer, spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good: for them is the final abode.﴾ ﴿Gardens of Eden, which they will enter, along with those who were righteous among their fathers, spouses and offspring. The angels will enter upon them from every gate.﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon you, for what you endured with patience. How excellent is the final abode!"﴾

Patience for the sake of God applies to calamities, illnesses, acts of worship, and restraint from desires and the like. The word "ibtighāʾ" (seeking) is in the accusative, either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or as an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). The word "wajh" (face) in this verse, in its apparent meaning, refers to the direction intended with God through good deeds so that the reward may fall upon them. This is like your saying, "The army went out for the sake of such-and-such." This is the most apparent meaning, though other possibilities are admitted. "Establishing the prayer" means performing it in its completeness, and "the prayer" here refers to the obligatory prayer.

His saying, "and spend," means giving to relieve the needy. "Secretly" refers to what is spent voluntarily (taṭawwuʿ), and "openly" refers to what is spent of the obligatory zakāt (the mandatory almsgiving), because it is best to be discreet with voluntary charity in general. His saying, ﴿and repel evil with good﴾, means that they repel with "that which is better" the one from whom they see something disliked. It was said that they repel with the statement "There is no god but God" the polytheism of others. It was also said that they repel with greeting (salām) the harms of people.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

In sum, they do not repay evil with evil. This is contrary to the conduct of the Jāhiliyya (the age of ignorance before Islam). It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning the Anṣār (the Helpers of Madina), and then it became general, after that, to everyone who possesses these qualities.

His saying, ﴿the final abode﴾, may mean the final outcome of the abode of this world. Then he explained "the outcome" with His saying, ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾, since "the outcome" encompasses both good and evil states. It may also mean: the outcome of the abode of the Hereafter for the abode of this world, that is, the outcome, the Garden in the Hereafter, belongs to them. The majority of readers recite "Jannāt ʿAdn" (Gardens of Eden). Al-Nakhaʿī recites "Jannatu ʿAdnin yudkhalūnahā" with a damma on the yāʾ and a fatḥa on the khāʾ. "Jannāt" is then a substitute (badal) for "ʿuqbā" and an explanation of it. "ʿAdn" (Eden) is the city of the Garden and its center. From it comes "Jannāt al-Iqāma" (Gardens of Abode), from ʿadana fī al-makān, meaning to remain in a place for a long time, and from it comes "maʿādin" (mines). It is said that Gardens of Eden are the dwelling only of the prophets, the martyrs and the scholars. This was said by ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, and it is related that it has five thousand gates.

His saying, ﴿and whoever was righteous﴾, means whoever did righteous deeds and believed. This was said by Mujāhid and others. It may also mean whoever was made fit for that by the decree of God and His foreknowledge. Al-Ṭabarī related, concerning the manner of the angels' entry, hadiths which we have not lengthened with, because their chains are weak. The meaning is: they say, "Peace be upon you," with the verb "they say" omitted for brevity and concision, since the apparent sense of the speech points to it. The meaning is: this is because of what you endured with patience. The meaning of ﴿the final abode﴾ follows the two meanings mentioned earlier. The majority read "fa-niʿma" with a kasra on the nūn and a sukūn on the ʿayn. Yaḥyā ibn Wathtāb read it with a fatḥa on the nūn and a kasra on the ʿayn. A group said: the meaning of ﴿the final abode﴾ is that they were given the Garden in return for Hell.

Al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is based on a hadith which has been transmitted: "Every man in Paradise had a known place in the Fire, but God diverted him from it to bliss. It is shown to him and it is said to him: 'This is the place of your seat.' So God replaces it for you with Paradise because of your faith, your obedience and your patience."

Ibn ʿAṭiyya on verses 22–24 of Sūrat al-Raʿd:

God Almighty says:

﴿Those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord, establish the prayer, spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good: for them is the final abode.﴾ ﴿Gardens of Eden, which they will enter, along with those who were righteous among their fathers, spouses and offspring. The angels will enter upon them from every gate.﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon you, for what you endured with patience. How excellent is the final abode!"﴾

The word "ibtighāʾ" (seeking) is in the accusative, either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or as an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). The word "wajh" (face) in this verse, in its apparent meaning, refers to the direction intended with God through good deeds so that the reward may fall upon them. This is like your saying, "The army went out for the sake of such-and-such." This is the most apparent meaning, though other possibilities are admitted. "Establishing the prayer" means performing it in its completeness, and "the prayer" here refers to the obligatory prayer.

"Secretly" refers to what is spent voluntarily (taṭawwuʿ), and "openly" refers to what is spent of the obligatory zakāt (the mandatory almsgiving), because it is best to be discreet with voluntary charity in general. It was said that they repel with the statement "There is no god but God" the polytheism of others. It was also said that they repel with greeting (salām) the harms of people.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 13, verse 25–29:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its binding, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth — for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. They rejoice in the life of this world, but the life of this world, compared with the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance."﴾ ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Surely, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds — joy (ṭūbā) is theirs, and a good final return.﴾

This is a description of a state opposed to the preceding one. Ibn Jurayj said, concerning the Exalted's saying ﴿and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾, that it was related: "If you do not walk to your relative with your feet, and do not comfort him with your wealth, then you have severed him." Mus'ab ibn Sa'd said: I asked my father about the Exalted's saying ﴿Say: Shall we inform you of those who are the greatest losers in deeds? Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 103–104]: are they the Harūriyya (Kharijites)? He said: No, but the Harūriyya are those who break the covenant of Allah after its binding, and he recited this verse. And Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, used to apply the two verses to them. "Al-la'na" (the curse) is distance from the mercy of Allah and from all good. ﴿Evil abode﴾ is the opposite of ﴿the good final abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24]. The more apparent meaning of "al-dar" here is that it is the abode of the Hereafter, though it is possible that it refers to this world, though with less strength.

As for the Exalted's saying ﴿Allah extends provision﴾, the verse: When the Exalted informed about those whose description preceded, that for them is the curse and the evil abode, He then turned after that to their wealthy and belittled their status and the status of their wealth. The meaning is that all of this is by the will of Allah: He grants wealth to the disbeliever in order to destroy him by it, and restricts it for the believer in order to magnify his reward and his treasure. The Exalted's saying "and restricts" (yaqdiru) means measuring out, and it is contrary to "extends" (yabsutu). Then He made them appear ignorant in His saying ﴿and they rejoice in the life of this world﴾, while it, in comparison with the Hereafter, is a fleeting, vanishing enjoyment, which is enjoyed a little and then perishes. "Matā'" (enjoyment) is that which is enjoyed and does not last. The poet said:

Enjoy, O disheveled one, for indeed a thing
that death has overtaken is but enjoyment.

The Exalted's saying ﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾: this is a refutation of those among the disbelievers of Quraysh who proposed signs, such as the sky falling upon them in pieces, and similar to their saying: "Move these two mountains away from us, make the valleys for us into farmland and gardens like al-Urdunn, and bring back to life for us Muḍayy and our forefathers." When that did not happen, it was because signs of demand do not, by custom, come through the prophets except when Allah wills to punish a people who said such a statement. So Allah replied to them: that is, the sending down of a sign does not necessarily entail your faith or your guidance; rather the matter is in the hand of Allah, who leads astray whom He wills, and guides to His obedience and to faith in Him whoever turns back to obedience and believes in the signs that give evidence. It is possible that the pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to the Noble Qur'an, or to Muhammad ﷺ.

"Alladhīna" is a substitution (badal) for "man" in the Exalted's saying ﴿whoever turns back﴾. The tranquility of hearts is submission, joy in the remembrance of Allah, tranquility in Him to the utmost degree, contentment with the reward from Him, and excellence of certainty. Then (p-203) the statement opens that the tranquility of hearts comes through the remembrance of Allah the Exalted. In this statement there is encouragement and incitement to faith. The meaning is: through this, tranquility is attained, not through the demanded signs; indeed, a people may disbelieve after them and then the punishment descends, as has preceded regarding some nations.

The second "alladhīna" is a new subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿ṭūbā lahum﴾. It is also permissible that "alladhīna" be a substitution for the first. "Ṭūbā" is a subject (ism) and "lahum" is its predicate. That "ṭūbā" is a subject is indicated by its being a mubtada'. It is of the form fu'lā from "al-ṭayyib" (the good), according to some of them. Sībawayh took it to the course of supplication and said: it is in the place of nominative case, and what indicates this is the nominative "wa-ḥusnu". Tha'lab said: it has been read "wa-ḥusna" with the accusative, so "ṭūbā" in this case is a verbal noun (maṣdar), as they say "saqyan laka" (watering for you), and its parallel among verbal nouns is "rujʿā" and "ʿuqbā".

Ibn Sayyida said: "ṭūbā" is the plural of ṭayyiba, according to Kurāʿ, and its parallel is Kūsā as the plural of kayyisa, and Ṣūfā as the plural of ṣayyifa.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The one who read "wa-ḥusna" with the accusative was Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Ibn Abi 'Abla.

The meaning of "ṭūbā" has been differed over. It was said: its meaning is "good for them." 'Ikrima said: its meaning is "blessed for them." al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: its meaning is "felicity for them." Ibn 'Abbas said: "ṭūbā" is the name of Paradise in Abyssinian. Sa'id ibn Mashjuh said: the name of Paradise is "ṭūbā" in Hindi. It was also said: "ṭūbā" is the name of a tree in Paradise, and with this the ḥadīths have been reported in succession. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Ṭūbā is a tree in Paradise; a rider who is diligent would travel in its shade for a hundred years without crossing it. Recite if you wish: ﴿and extended shade﴾ [al-Wāqiʿa: 30]."

Al-Ṭabarī related from Abu Hurayra, and from Mughith ibn Sumayy, and 'Utba ibn 'Abd, raising it, reports whose import is that this tree is not in any abode in Paradise except that there are some of its branches in it, that it bears fruit in the garments of the people of Paradise, and that horses come out from it with their saddles and bridles; and similar things whose chain has not been established.

"Al-ma'āb" means the return and the place of return, from "āba yaʾūbu". It is said of ṭūbā also: "ṭībā".

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 13, verse 25–29:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its binding, and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on the earth — for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾ ﴿Allah extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. They rejoice in the life of this world, but the life of this world, compared with the Hereafter, is nothing but a fleeting enjoyment.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "Why has no sign been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say: "Indeed, Allah leads astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back in repentance."﴾ ﴿Those who believe, and whose hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Surely, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.﴾ ﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds — joy (ṭūbā) is theirs, and a good final return.﴾

This is a description of a state opposed to the preceding one. Ibn Jurayj said, concerning the Exalted's saying ﴿and sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾, that it was related: "If you do not walk to your relative with your feet, and do not comfort him with your wealth, then you have severed him." Those whose effort is lost in the life of this world﴾ [al-Kahf: 103–104]: are they the Harūriyya (Kharijites)? He said: No, but the Harūriyya are those who break the covenant of Allah after its binding, and he recited this verse. "Al-la'na" (the curse) is distance from the mercy of Allah and from all good. ﴿Evil abode﴾ is the opposite of ﴿the good final abode﴾ [al-Ra'd: 24]. The more apparent meaning of "al-dar" here is that it is the abode of the Hereafter, though it is possible that it refers to this world, though with less strength.

As for the Exalted's saying ﴿Allah extends provision﴾, the verse: When the Exalted informed about those whose description preceded, that for them is the curse and the evil abode, He then turned after that to their wealthy and belittled their status and the status of their wealth. The meaning is that all of this is by the will of Allah: He grants wealth to the disbeliever in order to destroy him by it, and restricts it for the believer in order to magnify his reward and his treasure. The Exalted's saying "and restricts" (yaqdiru) means measuring out, and it is contrary to "extends" (yabsutu). Then He made them appear ignorant in His saying ﴿and they rejoice in the life of this world﴾, while it, in comparison with the Hereafter, is a fleeting, vanishing enjoyment, which is enjoyed a little and then perishes. Enjoy, O disheveled one, for indeed a thing
that death has overtaken is but enjoyment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 13, verses 30–32:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿Thus We have sent you to a nation before which other nations have passed away, so that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you, while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say: "He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return."﴾

﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains could be moved, or the earth could be split, or the dead could be made to speak, [it would be this Qur'an]. But to Allah belongs the affair entirely. Have not those who believe despaired that, if Allah willed, He would guide all of mankind? And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done, or it will descend close to their dwellings, until the promise of Allah comes. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾

﴿And messengers before you were mocked, but I gave respite to those who disbelieved, then I seized them. So how was My punishment?﴾

The kāf in His saying "kadhālika" (thus) is connected to the meaning in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back [in repentance]﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27]. That is, as Allah has carried out this, so have We sent you. This is one opinion. What appears to me is that the meaning is: just as We have established the custom that Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides, not by means of the proposed signs, so likewise is Our action with this nation. We sent you to them with revelation, not with the proposed signs. Thus Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made a treaty with them in the year of al-Hudaybiyya. He wrote the document, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." One of them said: "We do not recognize the Most Merciful, nor do we read His name."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What I say concerning this is that "al-Rahman" here refers to Allah, the Exalted, and His Essence. He attributed disbelief in Him to them absolutely. The story of al-Hudaybiyya and the story of Umayya ibn Khalaf with Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf concern only the refusal of the name and the evasion of this expression, which they knew only from Muhammad (ﷺ). Then Allah commanded His Prophet to declare the religion openly and to make the call clear, in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return."﴾ (p-205) And "al-matāb" means the place of return, like "al-ma'āb," because repentance (tawba) is return.

Then the meaning of the verse would be a report about them that they will not believe even if a Qur'an were revealed by which mountains could be moved or the earth split. This is the interpretation of al-Farra' and a group of interpreters. Another group said: rather, the answer to "law" (if) is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "if there were a Qur'an with such-and-such a description, they would not have believed in any way." Those who held this interpretation included Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and others, who said: "The disbelievers said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Remove the mountains from us, or move the two mountains of Makkah, for they have constricted us. Make for us land in plots for planting and tillage, and bring back to life for us our fathers and grandfathers, and so-and-so and so-and-so.' Then the verse was revealed" on this matter, informing that they would not believe even if all of that happened. Another group said: the answer to "law" is omitted, but it does not have this meaning. Rather its implied meaning is: "this Qur'an would have been the one by which this would be done." On this view, the verse includes the glorification of the Qur'an, and this is a good opinion that brings out the eloquence of the verse. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But to Allah belongs the affair entirely﴾ supports the last interpretation and is consistent with the others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired﴾ means: "do not know," and this is the dialect of Hawazin, as stated by al-Qasim ibn Ma'n. Ibn al-Kalbi said: it is the dialect of Hubayl, a tribe of al-Nakha'. From it is the verse of Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi:

؎ I say to them in the ravine when they drive me away: ∗∗∗ "Do you not know that I am the son of the knight Zahdam?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

(p-206) It is also possible that "despair" (al-ya's) in this verse is in its usual sense. This is because, when He had cast aside their faith in His saying: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an﴾ to the end of the verse, according to the two interpretations of the omitted and implied answer, He said in this: "Have not the believers despaired of the faith of these disbelievers, knowing that if Allah willed, He would guide all of mankind?"

Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read "ya'ys" (يَأْيَسْ). Ibn Abbas, Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Abi Mulayka, Ikrima, al-Jahdari, Ali ibn Husayn, Zayd ibn Ali, and Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "afalam yatabayyan" (أفَلَمْ يَتَبَيَّنْ), meaning "have they not made clear."

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs that they would not cease to be struck by calamities from the expeditions (sarāyā) and military campaigns (ghazawāt) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid read "wa-la yazālu alladhīna ẓalamū" (وَلا يَزالُ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا), "those who did wrong." Then He said: ﴿or it will descend close to their dwellings﴾, meaning: you, O Muhammad, will descend close to their homes. This is the interpretation of a group including al-Tabari, who attributed it to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the meaning is: "or the calamity will descend close to their dwellings." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid read "aw tahullu qarīban min diyārihim" (أو تَحُلُّ قَرِيبًا مِن دِيارِهِمْ) in the plural.

(p-207) The promise of Allah, according to Ibn Abbas and a group, is the conquest of Makkah. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the verse is general concerning the disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection, and the condition of the disbelievers is always thus, and the promise of Allah is the establishment of the Hour. "Al-qāri'a" is the calamity which strikes the heart of its possessor with its severity, such as killing, captivity, plunder of wealth, exposure of the women's sanctity, and the like.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And messengers before you were mocked﴾. This is a verse of consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: do not let your chest be constricted, O Muhammad, by what you see from your people and what you encounter from them, for that is not novel nor unprecedented. This has already occurred among earlier nations. "Amlaytu lahum" means: I extended the period and prolonged it. "Imlā'" is granting respite in the manner of gradual leading on (istidrāj), and it derives from "mulāwa" of time, as in "tamallaytu ḥasana al-ʿaysh" (I enjoyed a pleasant life).

His saying: ﴿So how was My punishment?﴾ is an affirmation and an expression of wonder, which contains within it a warning to the disbelievers contemporary with Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid read "wa-la yazālu alladhīna ẓalamū" (وَلا يَزالُ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا), "those who did wrong." Then He said: ﴿or it will descend close to their dwellings﴾, meaning: you, O Muhammad, will descend close to their homes. This is the interpretation of a group including al-Tabari, who attributed it to Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the meaning is: "or the calamity will descend close to their dwellings." Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid read "aw tahullu qarīban min diyārihim" (أو تَحُلُّ قَرِيبًا مِن دِيارِهِمْ) in the plural.

This has already occurred among earlier nations. "Amlaytu lahum" means: I extended the period and prolonged it. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 13, verses 30–32:

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿Thus We have sent you to a nation before which other nations have passed away, so that you may recite to them what We have revealed to you, while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say: "He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return."﴾

﴿And if there were a Qur'an by which mountains could be moved, or the earth could be split, or the dead could be made to speak, [it would be this Qur'an]. But to Allah belongs the affair entirely. Have not those who believe despaired that, if Allah willed, He would guide all of mankind? And those who disbelieve will not cease to be struck by a calamity for what they have done, or it will descend close to their dwellings, until the promise of Allah comes. Indeed, Allah does not fail in His promise.﴾

﴿And messengers before you were mocked, but I gave respite to those who disbelieved, then I seized them. So how was My punishment?﴾

The kāf in His saying "kadhālika" (thus) is connected to the meaning in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back [in repentance]﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27]. That is, as Allah has carried out this, so have We sent you. This is one opinion. What appears to me is that the meaning is: just as We have established the custom that Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides, not by means of the proposed signs, so likewise is Our action with this nation. We sent you to them with revelation, not with the proposed signs. Thus Allah leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾, Qatada and Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made a treaty with them in the year of al-Hudaybiyya. He wrote the document, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate." One of them said: "We do not recognize the Most Merciful, nor do we read His name."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What I say concerning this is that "al-Rahman" here refers to Allah, the Exalted, and His Essence. He attributed disbelief in Him to them absolutely. The story of al-Hudaybiyya and the story of Umayya ibn Khalaf with Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf concern only the refusal of the name and the evasion of this expression, which they knew only from Muhammad (ﷺ). Then Allah commanded His Prophet to declare the religion openly and to make the call clear, in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: "He is my Lord; there is no god but Him. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him is my return."﴾ (p-205) And "al-matāb" means the place of return, like "al-ma'āb," because repentance (tawba) is return.

Then the meaning of the verse would be a report about them that they will not believe even if a Qur'an were revealed by which mountains could be moved or the earth split. This is the interpretation of al-Farra' and a group of interpreters. Another group said: rather, the answer to "law" (if) is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "if there were a Qur'an with such-and-such a description, they would not have believed in any way." Those who held this interpretation included Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and others, who said: "The disbelievers said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Remove the mountains from us, or move the two mountains of Makkah, for they have constricted us. Make for us land in plots for planting and tillage, and bring back to life for us our fathers and grandfathers, and so-and-so and so-and-so.' Then the verse was revealed" on this matter, informing that they would not believe even if all of that happened. Another group said: the answer to "law" is omitted, but it does not have this meaning. Rather its implied meaning is: "this Qur'an would have been the one by which this would be done." On this view, the verse includes the glorification of the Qur'an, and this is a good opinion that brings out the eloquence of the verse. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But to Allah belongs the affair entirely﴾ supports the last interpretation and is consistent with the others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have not those who believe despaired﴾ means: "do not know," and this is the dialect of Hawazin, as stated by al-Qasim ibn Ma'n. Ibn al-Kalbi said: it is the dialect of Hubayl, a tribe of al-Nakha'. From it is the verse of Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi:

؎ I say to them in the ravine when they drive me away: ∗∗∗ "Do you not know that I am the son of the knight Zahdam?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

(p-206) It is also possible that "despair" (al-ya's) in this verse is in its usual sense. This is because, when He had cast aside their faith in His saying: ﴿And if there were a Qur'an﴾ to the end of the verse, according to the two interpretations of the omitted and implied answer, He said in this: "Have not the believers despaired of the faith of these disbelievers, knowing that if Allah willed, He would guide all of mankind?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 13, verses 33–35:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like those who associate partners with Allah]? Say, "Name them. Or do you inform Him of what He does not know on earth, or of [mere] outward speech?" Rather, the scheming of those who disbelieved has been made attractive to them, and they have been barred from the way. And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ ﴿For them is a punishment in the life of this world, but the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe, and they will have against Allah no protector.﴾ ﴿The example of Paradise which the righteous have been promised: beneath it rivers flow; its food is eternal and its shade [as well]. That is the final outcome of those who fear Allah, and the final outcome of the disbelievers is the Fire.﴾

In meaning, this verse refers back to His saying: ﴿while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Ra'd: 30]. The meaning is: Is He who is thus worthy of worship, or the inanimate objects that neither benefit nor harm? This is one interpretation. It appears, however, that the statement is connected to His saying: ﴿and they have set up for Allah partners﴾, as if the meaning were: Is He who possesses power and oneness, and to whom a partner is attributed, fit to take vengeance and punish, or not? "Souls" (al-anfus) are among His creatures, and He is "standing over every [soul]," i.e., encompassing it, so as to bring the admonition closer to the hearer's perception. Then He specified from the states of souls the state of their earning, so that a person, upon reflecting on the verse, would consider his deeds and his earnings.

His saying: ﴿Say, "Name them"﴾ means: name those who have attributes by which they deserve divinity. Then He turned away from speech and affirmed: Do you inform Allah of what He does not know? Al-Hasan recited "hal tunabbi'unahu" with a sukun on the nun and a light ba'. The "am" here has the meaning of "bal" together with the interrogative alif; this is the view of Sibawayh, and it is like the expression of the Arabs: "Indeed it is camels, or sheep?" Then He further affirmed, asking whether they intend to permit that by an outward matter? Because outward matters have a certain ambiguity and room for doubt, whereas what is merely outward speech has no basis for doubt at all. Al-Jumhur read "zuyyina" with the verb in the passive, and "makruhum" with a nominative; Mujahid read "zayyana" with the verb in the active, and "makrahum" with an accusative, i.e., Allah made it attractive. "Makruhum" is a term that encompasses their sayings and actions which were in opposition to the Sharia. 'Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-suddu" with a damma on the sad, which is in the transitive form; the rest read here and in "Ha Mim, the Believer" "wa-saddu" with a fatha, which may mean: they barred themselves, or they barred others. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "wa-siddu" with a kasra on the sad.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them is a punishment﴾ — the verse is a threat, i.e., for them is a punishment in their worldly life through killing, captivity, drought, and afflictions in their bodies, and other things by which Allah tests them. Then for them is a punishment more severe than all of this, which is being burned in the Fire. "Ashaqq" means more difficult, from "mashaqqa." "Al-waqi" is the one who shields in the manner of protection, from "wiqaya."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The example of Paradise﴾ — some said: "mathal" here means "description" (sifa), from your saying "mathhalt al-shay'" when you describe a thing to someone and bring his understanding of its matter close to him, not that it is a striking of a parable for it. It is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And to Him belongs the highest example﴾ [al-Rum: 27], i.e., the highest description. It appears that the meaning which forms in the soul as an image of Paradise is that rivers flow in it and that its food is eternal. Its nominative, according to Sibawayh, is implied; it was said its estimate is: "in what is recited to you or explicitly stated to you, [is] the example of Paradise." Its nominative according to al-Farra' is His saying "tajri," i.e., the description of Paradise is that rivers flow beneath it. Something similar exists in the speech of the Arabs. Some interpreted that "mathal" is superfluous (muqhamm), and that the estimate is: the Paradise which the righteous have been promised.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is unsound (qalaq). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn Mas'ud read "amthal al-jannah" (the examples of Paradise). The meaning of His saying ﴿beneath it rivers flow﴾ has been discussed more than once before.

His saying "ukuluha" means what is eaten therein. "Al-'uqba," "al-'aqiba," and "al-'aqib" mean a state that follows another state before it. The rest of the verse is clear.

It was also said: the estimate at the beginning of the verse is "the example of Paradise is a garden in which rivers flow," as al-Zajjaj said; the verse, according to this, is a parable for the Garden of bliss in the Hereafter.

(p-210) The Exalted's saying:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Scripture rejoice at what has been sent down to you, and among the factions there are those who deny part of it. Say: "I have only been commanded to worship God and not to associate anything with Him. To Him I call, and to Him is my return."﴾ ﴿And thus We sent it down as an Arabic judgment. If you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have no protector or defender against God.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent messengers before you and gave them wives and offspring. It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by God's leave. For every term there is a Book. God erases what He wills and confirms, and with Him is the Mother of the Book.﴾

The interpreters differed about who is meant by this verse. Ibn Zayd said: it refers to those among the People of the Book who believed, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his like.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is that God praises them for, because of the strength of their faith, being glad at what comes down to the Prophet ﷺ of the permissible rulings of the Law. Qatada said: it refers to all the believers. "The Book" is the Qur'an, and "what has been sent down to you" means the whole Law. Another group said: the intended meaning of "those to whom We gave the Scripture" is the Jews and Christians, because they rejoice at what is revealed to the Prophet ﷺ confirming their laws and mentioning their forefathers.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This interpretation is weak, because their concern with it is greater than their joy, so their joy is not counted. It is also weak because the Jews and Christians deny part of it, and God in this verse distinguishes between those who deny part of it and those to whom We gave the Scripture.

As for "the factions" (al-ahzab), Mujahid said they are the Jews, Christians and Magians. Another group said they are the factions of the Arabs of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period). God commanded him to disregard their disagreement, and to declare plainly that he was only commanded to worship God, to abandon associating partners with Him, to call to Him, and to believe in the return to Him, which is the return at the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment.

As for His saying "And thus": the meaning is: just as We made these people ready for joy and those people for denying part, thus [We sent it down as an Arabic judgment]. It may also be understood as: those to whom We gave the Scripture rejoice in it because of their understanding of it and the speed of their acceptance of it. Then He enumerated the blessing by saying "thus We made it," that is, We made it easy for them in this and We bestowed favour. "Judgment" (hukman) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). "Judgment" means the meanings contained in the Qur'an, and He made it Arabic because the expression of it is in Arabic. Then He addressed him, warning against following the desires of these misguided sects. The address is to Muhammad, upon whom be prayers and peace, but in meaning it encompasses the believers until the Day of Resurrection.
