When this expression concerns a matter that falls under the power of the one prohibited, it is a restraint; when it does not fall under his power, it is pure emphatic negation. The phrase ﴿by God's leave﴾ means: unless God grants permission in that.

As for His exalted saying: ﴿For every term there is a Book﴾, it is a general expression covering all things that have terms (ajal). That is because nothing exists in them without having a term at its beginning and at its end, and every term is written and limited. God informed us of His writing the terms that belong to things in general. Al-Dahhak and al-Farra' said: the meaning is "for every Book there is a term."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This reversal is not necessary and has no basis, since the meaning is complete in the order of the Qur'an. Indeed, their statement can be refuted by pointing out that things which God wrote as eternal and lasting, such as the bliss of the people of Paradise and other things, have a Book but no term.

As for His exalted saying: ﴿God erases what He wills and confirms﴾, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wayuthabbit" with a doubled bā' (shaddah); Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read it with a single bā'. People have been confused about the meanings of these words, and what clarifies the difficulty is this: we should believe that the things God decreed in eternity and knew in a certain state are not subject to erasure or change; these are what is written in the Mother of the Book and what decree has preceded. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others among the people of knowledge. As for the things which God has informed us He changes and transfers, such as forgiving sins after they have been established, and abrogating (naskh) a verse after its recitation while its ruling has become settled, then erasure and confirmation occur in them, in what the recording angels record and the like. As for when the matter is referred to destiny and decree, God has erased what He erased and confirmed what He confirmed. The expression came in the future tense, concerning the erasure of events, and these matters belong to what is yet to take place in time, so that human beings await what He will erase or confirm; their fear, hope and supplication accord with that. A group, including al-Hasan, said: it concerns the terms of the children of Adam. That is because God, on the Night of Decree (and it is said: the Night of the middle of Sha'ban) writes the terms of the dead, so some people are erased from the register of the living and recorded in the register of the dead. Qays ibn 'Ubad said: the tenth of Rajab is the day on which God erases what He wills and confirms.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This specification in the terms or in other matters has no meaning. What is appropriate here among the sayings is only what is general to all things. Among these is that the meaning of the verse is: God changes affairs according to their states, that is, what is by nature liable to change, as we have stated before, so He erases from that state and confirms it in the state to which He transfers it. It is reported from 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud that they used to say in their supplication: "O God, if You have recorded us in the register of wretchedness, then erase us and confirm us in the register of happiness, for You erase what You will and confirm." (p-213) This is a supplication for the forgiveness of sins and expresses anxiety on their part. That is: O God, if we have been wretched through Your disobedience, and sins and wretchedness have been written against us, then erase them from us through forgiveness and obedience. In one version of the words of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, something of this appears. Their supplication was by no means about altering what was decreed beforehand, and that should not be interpreted against them.

It has also been said: this verse was revealed because when the Quraysh heard God's saying: ﴿It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by God's leave﴾, they said: "Muhammad has no power or share in this matter." So the verse came down: ﴿God erases what He wills and confirms﴾, that is: perhaps God grants permission in such a matter, as you dislike, after He had not been granting permission.

Al-Tabari reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "God erases what He wills and confirms among the affairs of His servants, except happiness, wretchedness and the terms, for there is no erasure in them."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is close to what we established at the beginning concerning the verse.

It is also reported from a group that they said: God erases what He wills and confirms from a Book, except the Mother of the Book which is with Him and which He does not change at all. Another group said: the meaning is: He erases everything He wills and confirms everything He intends. These sayings are easily refuted. Al-Tabari transmitted, via Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, that Ka'b said to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab: "O Commander of the Faithful, were it not for a verse in the Book of God I would inform you of what will occur until the Day of Resurrection." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God erases what He wills and confirms, and with Him is the Mother of the Book﴾." Abu al-Ma'ali mentioned in al-Talkhis that 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, was the one who said this statement attributed to Ka'b; in my view, that is not authentic from 'Ali.

The interpreters' expressions also differed in explaining "the Mother of the Book." Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: it is the Reminder (al-dhikr). Ka'b said: it is God's knowledge of what He will create and what His creatures will do.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The most correct explanation of "the Mother of the Book" is that it is the register of newly occurring affairs regarding which the decree has already preceded with what will be, and it has preceded that they would not be changed; while erasure and confirmation remain in affairs which the decree has preceded will be changed, erased and confirmed. Qatada said something similar. Another group said: the meaning of "the Mother of the Book" is the lawful and the unlawful. This is the saying of al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 13, verses 40–43:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Whether We show you some of what We promise them, or We take you (in death), your duty is only to deliver the message, and upon Us is the reckoning.﴾ ﴿Have they not seen that We come to the land, reducing it from its borders? And Allah judges; there is none to repel His judgment, and He is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿Those before them had already plotted, but to Allah belongs all plotting. He knows what every soul earns, and the disbelievers will come to know to whom the ultimate abode belongs.﴾ ﴿Those who disbelieve say, "You are not a messenger." Say, "Allah suffices as a witness between me and you, and (so does) whoever has knowledge of the Book."﴾

"In" (إنْ) is a conditional particle, to which "ma" (ما) has been attached, and it precedes the verb. Thus it becomes, in this respect, equivalent to the emphatic lam (اللام المؤكدة) of the oath that comes before the verb, as in your saying: "By Allah, you will certainly go out" (واللهِ لَتَخْرُجَنَّ). For this reason it is good for the heavy nun (النون الثقيلة) to enter in your saying "nurayannaka" (نُرِيَنَّكَ), since it occupies here the place of the lam there. Had "ma" not been attached, that would not be permissible except in poetry.

"Some" (البعض) is singled out for mention, since it is understood that lifespans fall short of witnessing everything that the decrees bring of what the disbelievers are promised; and likewise He gave existence (to the promise). Do you not see that most of the conquests occurred after the Prophet (ﷺ)? And "aw" (أوَ) is a conjunction of alternation.

His saying "fa-innama" (فَإنَّما) is the response of the condition. The meaning of the verse: if you remain, O Muhammad, to see it, or We take you (in death) (p-215), then in both cases your duty is only to deliver the message. His saying "naʿiduhum" (نَعِدُهُمْ) may mean by it the harms with which the disbelievers were threatened; he used the word "promise" for them since those harms were known and explicitly stated. It may also mean the promise to Muhammad (peace be upon him) of the destruction of disbelief, and then he attributed the promise to them because it concerned their affair.

The pronoun in His saying "yarawu" (يَرَوْا) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, whose pronoun was previously mentioned in His saying "naʿiduhum". His saying "We come to the land" (نَأْتِي الأرْضَ) means: by power and command, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah came at their structure from its foundations﴾ [al-Nahl: 26]. "The land" (الأرض) here refers to the generic noun; it is also said that it refers to the land of the aforementioned disbelievers, and this is according to the difference in His saying "nanquṣuhā min aṭrāfihā" (نَنْقُصُها مِن أطْرافِها). The majority read "nanquṣuhā" (نَنْقُصُها), and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "nunaqqiṣuhā" (نُنَقِّصُها). As for His saying "min aṭrāfihā" (مِن أطْرافِها), whoever said that it is the land of the aforementioned disbelievers said: its meaning is, have they not seen that We come to the land of these people with victory for you, and reduce it by what enters your religion from the tribes and the neighboring lands? So what secures them that We will not empower you over them too, as We did with their neighbors? This was said by Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and this view can only hold if the revelation of this verse is assumed to have been in Medina. Whoever said that "the land" (الأرض) is a generic noun took the reduction from its borders to mean the ruin of the buildings that Allah brings upon the disbelievers. This is also the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid. A group said: the reduction is by the death of people, the perishing of fruits, and the loss of blessing; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās also, al-Shaʿbī, ʿIkrima, and Qatāda. Another group said: the reduction is by the death of the righteous and the scholars; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbās also and Mujāhid. All of these are included in the wording of the verse. The "ṭaraf" (الطرف) of anything is its best part, and from this is the saying of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him: "Knowledge is valleys; whichever valley you take from it, you will be deprived, so take from every thing its ṭaraf (طرفًا)," meaning its best. The gist of the meaning of this verse is admonition and the striking of parables, i.e., have they not seen, so that admonition would occur from them? The most fitting intent of the wording of the verse is the diminishing of the land through the conquests won by Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying "lā muʿaqqiba" (لا مُعَقِّبَ) means: there is no one who repels or contradicts, who follows up His judgments, i.e., who looks into their consequences to see whether they are a misfortune or not. The swiftness of Allah's reckoning is necessary, because by His encompassing knowledge it is not by counting.

(p-216) "Makr" (المَكْر) is what devises against a person and schemes against him, whether or not he is aware of it. Allah the Exalted described the nations that schemed against their prophets, just as Quraysh schemed against Muhammad (ﷺ). His saying "fa-lillāhi al-makru jamīʿan" (فَلِلَّهِ المَكْرُ جَمِيعًا) means: the punishments He brought upon them, and He named them "makr" according to the usage of naming the punishment by the name of the sin, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqara: 15] and similar. In His saying "yaʿlamu mā taksibu kullu nafs" (يَعْلَمُ ما تَكْسِبُ كُلُّ نَفْسٍ) there is an alert and a warning embedded within a report. Then He, blessed and exalted, threatened them with His saying: ﴿And the disbelievers will come to know to whom the ultimate abode belongs﴾. Nafiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, and Abū ʿAmr read "al-kāfir" (الكافِرُ) in the singular, as a generic noun. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī read "al-kuffār" (الكُفّارُ). Ibn Masʿūd read "al-kāfirūn" (الكافِرُونَ), and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read "alladhīna kafarū" (الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا). The discussion of "ʿuqbā al-dār" (عُقْبى الدارِ) has preceded this.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Those who disbelieve say...﴾ The verse. The meaning: these disbelievers deny you, O Muhammad, and say: you are not sent by Allah; you are merely a claimant. Say to them: ﴿Allah suffices as a witness﴾. "Billāh" (بِاللهِ) is in the place of nominative, the implied sense being: Allah suffices. "Shahīd" (شَهِيدٌ) means "shāhid" (witness). His saying: ﴿and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾ — it was said: he means the Jews and Christians who possess the earlier scriptures that speak of rejecting idols and the Oneness of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted. He means those among them who believed, such as ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, Tamīm al-Dārī, and Salmān al-Fārisī, who testify to the truth of Muhammad (peace be upon him). Mujāhid said: he means ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām specifically; he said: "It was revealed concerning me: ﴿and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These last two views cannot stand unless the verse is Medinan, whereas the majority hold that it is Meccan. This was said by Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, who said: it cannot be that the verse concerns ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām, because it is Meccan; and he used to read: ﴿and whoever has knowledge of the Book﴾.

(p-217) It was also said: he means Allah the Exalted, as if He invoked Allah, glorified be He, as a witness, then mentioned Him with these words which contain an attribute of exaltation. This view is objected to on the ground that it involves coordinating an attribute with the thing described, which is not permissible; attributes are only coordinated with one another. It is also possible that "min" (مِن) is in the place of nominative as a subject, with the predicate omitted, the sense being: "more just and more binding in statement," and similar to this, what the word "shahīdan" indicates, and it means Allah the Exalted.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrima, Mujāhid, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥakam, and others read: "wa-min ʿindihi ʿilmu al-kitāb" (وَمِن عِنْدِهِ عِلْمُ الكِتابِ) with a kasra on the mīm of "min" and a kasra on the dāl, lowering the dāl. Abū al-Fatḥ said: this was also transmitted from the Prophet (peace be upon him). ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib also read, as did al-Ḥasan and Ibn al-Samayfaʿ: "wa-min ʿindihi ʿulima al-kitābu" (وَمِن عِنْدِهِ عُلِمَ الكِتابُ), with a kasra on the mīm and the dāl, a damma on the ʿayn and a kasra on the lām in the passive form, and "al-kitābu" in the nominative. These readings intend Allah the Exalted, and their wording admits no other meaning.

The Commentary on Surah al-Ra'd is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah bless our master Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, and his family and companions.
